The proposed descriptor includes a binary feature that distinguishes between the sign of the Laplacian operator's results, making it immune to image inversion and 3D transformations that reverse spatial coordinates, achieving SP-symmetry or SP-invariance. This generalization of symmetry applies to arbitrary scalar image fields and encompasses well-known CP-symmetry seen in charged elementary particles. Local feature orientation is represented as a set of independent states accounting for possible reflections, irrespective of image intensity inversion. Two key axis vectors are derived from observed image data, along with a third axial vector defined by the right-hand rule. Adding the sign component to the traditional geometry of local features (location, scale, orientation) generates descriptors that are robust to global orientation and 3D spatial axis inversions. These enhanced feature geometry properties streamline the matching of local features in 3D volumetric images, eliminating the need to estimate local feature orientation and achieving global 3D feature correspondence. This leads to a registration algorithm that is more robust and efficient, particularly for sparse datasets, as demonstrated by our experimental results. The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal, English language-independent manner. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a graph-based structure, allowing for the generation of highly detailed, typically lengthed narratives that are also easier to understand. Our research shows that TCube outperforms existing methods in both fluency and sense, according to human evaluations, by 19% and 34% respectively, while also being more adaptable to different domains. For example, we can modify TCube to create Chinese narratives by simply redefining the vocabulary without further adjustments. Furthermore, we conducted a consumer behavior analysis case study that demonstrates the benefits of TCube for making sales forecasts more accessible and understandable to consumers. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Notably, this study's findings indicate that an LSTM cell outperforms a GRU cell in the selected experiments. To validate the proposed model's ability to capture long-term dependencies, this study conducts an analysis of the estimated character probabilities. This study also delves into the significance of global context in Japanese word segmentation through a dimensionality reduction technique known as t-Distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding (t-SNE). To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow and involves analyzing a substantial sample of links, exploring their data sources, and examining the users involved in repeated sharing activities. This in-depth examination aims to uncover the underlying logic behind users' decision-making process when selecting external resources to share, ultimately providing insights that can inform future knowledge management practices. Our data analysis uncovers that a small subset of users contributes significantly to the sharing of recurring external links and also reveals that links to programming-related knowledge repositories, such as GitHub and GitBash, as well as official documentation and academic sources, such as Wikipedia, are over-represented in users' repetitive sharing efforts. Furthermore, our results indicate that users with higher levels of experience and expertise also engage in repeated sharing activities, focusing on a limited range of widely recognized, reliable external sources. This study paves the way for future research to develop automated approaches for identifying and labeling this shared knowledge, ultimately facilitating users' knowledge management and augmenting the existing knowledge base on Stack Overflow. Additionally, our results may inspire the design of new interface features on the platform to better support users' collaborative knowledge management efforts. Furthermore, our research can be potentially extended to other knowledge communities to explore the nuances of external link sharing within diverse social media platforms and communities. Lastly, the analytical framework developed in this study can be employed to investigate other types of shared knowledge, such as text and media, to further enhance the collaborative knowledge base on Stack Overflow. Observations suggest a potential relationship between a galaxy's brightness and its central dark matter, indicating the need for a more comprehensive explanation. This study investigates various theoretical models that account for galaxy diversity, comparing their performance to a control model with no dark matter. Using a large dataset of 96 real-life galaxies, we evaluate the effectiveness of different models in matching observed rotation curves. However, our analysis reveals that none of the traditional dark matter models successfully match the observed curves when compared to a control model with no dark matter. On the other hand, strong dark matter models that incorporate anisotropic halos or "teasers" by potentially anomalous galaxies exhibit better match. Moreover, using Bayesian inference on anisotropic halo models, we find that the central density of dark matter drops to approximately 1 percent of its initial value at a distance equal to the optical radius, thus favoring weak dark matter models. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that if galaxies follow a standard mass-dark matter relation, then the contribution of dark matter to galactic rotation should follow a consistent pattern regardless of the galaxy's initial mass. resulting in slow implementation of the necessary societal changes to mitigate its effects.
To enhance climate communication and promote individual actions, we are developing a system
that leverages climate information tailored to each person's values. To overcome initial adoption hurdles,
our system employs a vast knowledge base that maps climate causes and effects to relevant personal values.
Given the absence of a complete climate knowledge base, we revisit knowledge acquisition techniques and construct
a database through natural language analysis of publicly available sources. To foster further research and applications,
the knowledge base and its code will be made open-source for the scientific community. In a preliminary study,
we tested our system's effectiveness in promoting climate conversation using a self-administered survey with 173 participants. 

Our key findings reveal that people are more likely to engage in climate conversations when the connection between values and causes is clarified,
especially for individuals who initially consider climate change an insignificant personal issue.
To further optimize our system, future work will involve refining the climate knowledge base through additional human annotations

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specialties. 
To reduce dependency on specific data, we develop an adaptive transformer-based symptom extraction model, incorporating a proprietary scoring system that filters and consolidates relevant information from unlabelled records. 
Also, our pre-trained language model is pre-conditioned using medical information, allowing it to grasp the underlying connections between various symptoms more effectively. 
Experimental findings on a large dataset of cardiac surgery records demonstrate the significant generalization capabilities of our approach. 
By applying the trained model on unlabelled records, we are able to accurately identify symptoms in unseen patient data with an accuracy of 42.7%. 
Additionally, our approach exhibits improved performance when compared to a model that has been fine-tuned on a separate, separate dataset. 
This development has a significant potential to make extracted information widely accessible across different medical settings and professionals. 
The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/grasmick/forget.

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Additionally, we determined several thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark stars, such as adiabatic index, bulk viscosity, and entropy, in addition to evaluating the stability of these stars in relation to causality constraints and their tidal deformability. Our findings show that increasing the magnetic field and temperature result in a decrease in the radius and increase in the tidal deformability of spin-polarized strange quark stars. However, a rise in the polarization of quarks leads to a decrease in the radius but an increase in the tidal deformability of these stars. We also observed that the properties of spin-polarized strange quark stars are significantly influenced by the magnetic field but to a lesser extent by the polarization of quarks. Furthermore, we found that the mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars lies within the range of $\sim 0.0929$ to $0.1016$ M$_\odot$. A graphical analysis revealed that the effects of a strong magnetic field on the properties of spin-polarized strange quark stars are comparable to those observed in non-polarized strange quark stars. We also constructed an energy profile of a spin-polarized strange quark star across varying temperatures and magnetic fields, and found that increasing the magnetic field and temperature result in a decrease in the energy of these stars. Moreover, we found that the energy of spin-polarized strange quark stars becomes negative at a certain radius, and that their energy is predominantly negative due to the contribution of the magnetic pressure term. Our study also shows that the total energy of these stars is the sum of the gravitational pressure term and the magnetic pressure term. We derived an equation to describe the correlation between temperature and magnetic field strength at the surface of spin-polarized strange quark stars, and found that increasing the magnetic field strength results in a rise in the surface temperature of these stars. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe. Experimental results show that Pando's throughput and efficiency significantly surpass those of existing alternative solutions. For instance, when rendering the iconic Schwarzenberg Castle using ray tracing, Pando's average generation time was nearly 10 times that of a local GPU, while its memory usage remained under 20% of the available system memory. Our findings indicate that Pando's decentralized architecture and efficient code management enable successful parallelism rates and efficient outcome generation, thus paving the way for a range of novel applications in the field of distributed computing. These applications could also lead to novel distributed algorithms. Additionally, Pando's novel architecture can serve as a distributed programming paradigm, and as such, is positioned as a significant contribution to the field of computer science. Pando's source code is publicly available under the BSD license, and as such, is cross-platform compatible, and can be accessed at: https://pando.js/. Also, a detailed documentation of the project is hosted at: http://pando.js/. Finally, the project's Web of Computers, comprising a range of computational resources, and which powered our evaluation, is publicly accessible at: http://pando.js/. It can be easily utilized for evaluating the performance of other distributed computing and volunteer computing-based solutions. It is worth noting that the project's goals, and particularly its focus on and approach to decentralized computing, differ from, and even counter, the trend of utilizing cloud services. Moreover, the project's goals are aligned with and akin to those of Distributed.net, and especially its Prime95 program, though both were unknown to us at the time of development. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. The authors' evaluation, encompassing various scenarios, demonstrates significant performance gains, while also outlining possible avenues for future research to further enhance Flatee's security and efficiency properties, particularly regarding attacks on the aggregation process and the balance between training speed and security. Factors such as environmental unpredictability, limited hardware availability, and costs often hinder effective testing. To address these issues, this research presents a novel testing framework that targets driver verification on microcontrollers. The proposed solution involves a device under test, a duplicating counterpart, and a central control unit. The control unit manages testing procedures while the device under test runs the code being tested and its counterpart simulates the interactions with external peripherals. The effectiveness of the solution was validated through various test protocols. The advantages of the solution include its ability to conduct arbitrary driver testing, mitigate the influence of external environments, and eliminate the need for external hardware counterparts. The results show that the solution can finish testing within 1-2 seconds and the involved hardware components can be recycled for other testing procedures after each test cycle. Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact, high-quality forms involve the product space form, incorporating product Bergman and polydisc structures. We examine the applicability of linear classifiers trained using supervised learning in these complex product spaces. We illustrate the difficulties of training linear classifiers with traditional methods like logistic regression or support vector machines, resulting in inconsistent results. We introduce a novel approach, combining ideas from kernel methods and positive definite functions, to address this issue. This new approach ensures the classifier is consistently applied across the complex product space. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method using two key datasets: classification of natural images in RGB and spectral color formats and a dataset of wordless audiobooks. This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize the computational burden of learning tasks. We focus on independent component analysis through a compressive lens, demonstrating that certain properties within the cumulant-based ICA model yield a compact set of solutions that can be effectively represented within the cumulant tensor space. Utilizing a property that ensures randomness and coherence, we establish the existence of a compressive ICA scheme and propose two novel algorithms, IPG and ASD, to realize the compressed order through experimental verification. To enhance magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in cavity magnomechanics, we develop an approach incorporating a coherent feedback loop. Furthermore, our findings confirm that both the steady and dynamic behaviors of this system can generate genuine tripartite entanglement. We establish that when the cavity is in the single-photon regime and the mechanical system is in a state of coherent quantum state, the magnon-photon-phonon entanglement is maximized with a coherent feedback loop. We also demonstrate that in the strong coupling regime, the entanglement of the system is primarily attributed to the magnon-photon component. Moreover, the proposed method enables the observation of tripartite entanglement not only in the steady state but also in the dynamic behavior of the system. We evaluate the effects of feedback noise and find that a minimal amount of feedback noise can be tolerated without significantly altering the entanglement of the system. We also show that the entanglement of the system is resistant to thermal phonon effects and that this entanglement can be restored through the application of a strong magnetic field. Our study has the potential to advance research in magnon-photon-phonon entanglement and contribute to the development of novel magnomechanical quantum technologies. We also propose an experimentally feasible approach for the implementation of the coherent feedback loop using current technological capabilities. We have obtained one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for color and spin spaces, applicable to all five scenarios: $q \to qq'\bar{q}'$, $q \to qq\bar{q}$, $q \to qgg$, $g \to gq\bar{q}$ and $g \to ggg$. The exact expressions are derived within dimensionless QCD and include the results of a specific integral up to its second-order expansion. Additionally, we have evaluated the associated splitting functions. Our results are crucial and necessary for creating subtraction and integrated-subtraction terms in next-to-next-to-next-to leading order cross-section computations. Moreover, we have carried out a detailed comparison of our results with two other approaches based on soft-collinear effective theory and cohomology techniques, finding agreement up to the one-loop level. Our work also addresses an apparent issue in one of these approaches which could lead to the wrong coefficient of the $1/\epsilon^3$ term in the dimensionless QCD procedure. The key issue is related to the sector-improved effective theory not being able to produce a certain non-form factor part of the triple-collinear operator, indicating a possible missing contribution from a DGLAP-like equation. This could also affect the understanding of running couplings in general and potentially influence the development of NNLLl+T terms in cross-section computations, particularly those related to top-quark processes. Lastly, we have expressed all necessary constants in terms of standard four-dimensional QCD and derived a new expression for the $q \to qq\bar{q}$ splitting function which is completely numerical and can be evaluated with just one unknown constant. This constant is related to a double-box integral which is yet to be numerically evaluated. Moreover, we have obtained an interesting expression for the $q \to qgg$ splitting function which is completely numerical and only requires knowledge of two constants, one of which is a well-known constant and the other is a constant related to a double-box integral which is yet to be numerically evaluated. This result is interesting because it reveals that the splitting function only depends on one constant which is related to a box integral, provided some certain conditions are met. Finally, we have obtained an interesting expression for the $g \to gq\bar{q}$ splitting function which is completely numerical and only requires knowledge of two constants, one of which is a well-known constant and the other is a constant related to a double-box integral which is yet to be numerically evaluated

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated and applied to one-dimensional local rings, and this concept is currently being used within Singular software implementation. Furthermore, a relevant theorem based on Greenberg's Strong Approximation theorem has also been introduced and applied to the realm of one-dimensional local rings. This has also led to the development of a method to compute the direct summands of finite $p$-polarized abelian groups over one-dimensional local rings. Additionally, a formula for computing the trace function of a finite $p$-polarized abelian group over a one-dimensional local ring has been established. Finally, a formula to calculate the ramification index of a finite $\mathbb{Q}_p$-extension $(\mathbb{Q}_p(S))_{\mathrm{ram}}$ has been derived. 

Please note that this work relies heavily on the concepts and results presented in a previously published paper titled ``Formal proof of the Neron Desingularization, a Multidimensional Case Algorithm'', however the current paper introduces new and novel ideas not present in that paper. 

In order to facilitate the development of this work, various essential tools were introduced and applied, including a construction method for finite type $\mathbb{Q}_p$-algebras over one-dimensional local rings, and a formula for computing the trace function of a finite type $\mathbb{Q}_p$-algebra over a one-dimensional local ring. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  Additionally, we show that the closure complement problem for the specific context can be solved by examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of particular triangle-free graph types. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources is currently not well understood. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), researchers discovered a first-of-its-kind correlation between the spectral indices and brightness temperatures of solar noise storm sources. They found that the sources with higher spectral indices tend to be brighter. Additionally, the study revealed that the sources exhibiting higher spectral indices and higher brightness temperatures are typically located farther from the solar equator, suggesting that these storm sources are associated with twisted magnetic field structures known as coronal holes and bipolar active regions. The discovery of this correlation is consistent with the theory that the acceleration of particles during solar noise storms is often linked to microflares driven by the twisting and reconnection of magnetic field flux ropes. The study's findings provide new insights into the dynamic evolution of solar noise storm sources and the complex magnetic field dynamics of active regions. These insights will contribute to a greater understanding of the basic physical processes governing the formation and behavior of these flux structures, which are key to explaining the quiet-time noise storm phenomenon observed in radio data from near-Earth active regions. The discovery may also be relevant to the study of similar stellar noise storm phenomena and the development of more advanced exotic particle models that could explain some anomalous cosmic ray observations. The research may also be helpful in informing the development of future observational facilities, such as the next-generation Low-frequency Array (LOFAR), which will be used to study the solar system and nearby galaxies at low frequencies. The research will be influential in informing the development of future solar and magnetic field observational facilities. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity. Furthermore, this design features simplified alignment and a more robust configuration due to the integrated grating and magnetic fields. The efficiency of the trap was evaluated through experiments and theoretical simulations, demonstrating excellent agreement between the results. This planar-integrated MOT has the potential to be a vital component in the development of compact quantum systems. Due to its small size, this design is suitable for a broad range of applications, from atomic clock networks to quantum communication systems. It also has the potential to be an essential part of the development of the first commercial quantum clock, the Si28 clock. This design leverages the unique characteristics of the 13-line system to achieve an unprecedented level of stability, accuracy, and resolution, along with the longest storage duration and fastest switching capabilities. It has the potential to significantly advance the performance of atomic clocks while meeting the size requirements of the specific application. Therefore, this planar-integrated MOT design not only meets but also exceeds the specifications of the Si28 clock, indicating great potential for the widespread use of this design in the quantum technology community. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving a substantial reduction in computational complexity. Additionally, the LSTM-based estimator for IEEE 802.11p demonstrates superior channel tracking capabilities in various testing environments. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and evaluating the generated images against the real data distribution using the Frechet inception distance (FID) metric. The experimentally determined optimal learning rate is 0.0002, and the assessment is performed on the Astronomical Image Colorization (AIC) dataset consisting of 300 high-resolution images and 300 low-resolution images, both derived from the Raw Image dataset. We demonstrate that our model can effectively colorize images by incorporating random noise as input, and upscaling low-resolution images to higher resolutions by inputting those lower-resolution images into our model. The proposed architecture outperforms the comparison model, producing better results in terms of performance and aesthetic appeal. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub, and the generated colorized and high-resolution images are posted on the AIC website. We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for handwritten digits. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby ensuring the reliability of the weight calculations. As a direct consequence, the algorithm's computational speed surpasses that of traditional ANN training methods by at least two orders of magnitude. In a comparative study, we observed that the development of an ANN with 70-80 weights using our approach took approximately 0.7-0.8 seconds, whereas other methods required around 0.2-0.3 seconds for comparable calculations. Nonetheless, the proposed algorithm's primary advantage lies in its ability to efficiently calculate ANN weights for extremely large datasets. It is also highly versatile and can be applied to solve a wide range of complex mathematical and statistical problems. The algorithm's performance is attributed to the inherent properties of the approximation matrices, which not only ensure the correctness of the weight calculations but also facilitate the development of highly accurate ANN solutions. In a related study, we characterized the properties of these matrices and established precise error bounds for their inversion, thereby paving the way for the development of a wide range of novel numerical algorithms. This work is an extension of the author's PhD thesis. One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning environment involving both humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on local edge computing and AI-driven processes at multiple robotic platforms to generate a unified, AI-driven global model that is shared across the network, and utilizes human-robot interaction instances to inform learning. This innovative framework extends the traditional LfD approach to encompass multi-agent settings, incorporates human learning within existing robotic frameworks, and incorporates advanced AI methodologies to model interdependencies between robotic tasks, and it demonstrates its applicability through the implementation of a realistic industrial case study in a dynamic agile production system that recovers critical raw materials. Experimental results show that the multi-agent LfD approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques and successfully addresses the challenges of complex collaborative learning in large-scale environments. This research will be made publicly available under an open-source license, and it is expected to pave the way for the development of robust and open cognitive AI architectures that can facilitate multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy in human-robot collaborative systems. A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this new estimator is designed to apply to the median regression model, making it a valuable tool in modern data analysis.  Theoretical performance of the estimator has been evaluated, showing that it achieves the same rate of bias reduction as existing methods but with reduced bias.  Through simulations, the new estimator has been shown to outperform existing methods.  Additionally, the utility of the estimator has been demonstrated via analysis of real-world datasets.  A related method of bias-corrected estimation for quantiles has also been proposed, providing a valuable alternative to existing strategies.  The theoretical results have been complemented with a proof of consistency for a specific quantile regression model, filling a notable gap in existing literature. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. Our experimental results reveal a notable increase
in F1 scores of 3.7% and 2.3% on the TAC3030 and Wikidata entities datasets
respective, along with a notable reduction in error rates of up to 5.2%. Furthermore,
we provide code and model implementations at https://github.com/asharakeh/RE-KGP.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustrations, caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, leading to distinct behaviors. This unique scenario represents a rare occurrence where the two species in a binary system interact differently due to distinct interactions with a third component, resulting in the peculiar disordered state. This phenomenon is further accentuated by the presence of spin correlations extending beyond the immediate neighborhood. Moreover, the crystals exhibited anomalies in their electrical resistivity at the magnetic transition points, with the resistivity being higher in Tb3RuO7 due to the magnetic frustrations. We have also conducted theoretical calculations to confirm the accuracy of our experimental findings. In summary, the unique magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7, characterized by magnetic frustrations, lead to distinct physical properties. In contrast, the ordered magnetic patterns in Nd3RuO7 result in typical physical properties. Therefore, the crystals of Tb3RuO7 possess inherent complexities, facilitated by the magnetic interactions with the neighboring atoms, resulting in the unique disordered state and magnetic frustrations. In turn, these factors result in the distinctive physical properties, needing to be addressed in further studies. Instead of the typical quantum systems exhibiting the unique disordered state at low temperatures, the crystals of Tb3RuO7 exhibit this state at a relatively higher temperature of 40 K, due to the external magnetic interactions. In conclusion, the unique disordered state in Tb3RuO7 is an extraordinary example, primarily caused by the differing internal magnetic fields imposed by the ordered terbium atoms on the two ruthenium species, resulting in the magnetic frustrations. Multi-layer neural networks are capable of forming complex representations of a signal, but dependent on extensive training data. We investigate whether these complex representations can also be learned with limited, domain-specific data, generating localized functional representations of a signal. We introduce an analysis-friendly architecture incorporating modulated periodic activations (MPAs) into neural networks, effectively constraining high-dimensional global representations to more manageable local functional representations. Utilizing a novel training objective, we demonstrate the MPA architecture efficiently generates local representations applicable across a wide range of image and video classification tasks, even with minimal labeled data. The periodized nature of these representations also facilitates interpretative results, with the added benefit of significantly reducing the computational requirements of inference. We evaluate the MPA architecture on various classification tasks, matching and outperforming previous method results while providing comparable if not better interpretability. The modulated periodic activations have now been implemented in an open-source PyTorch repository. https://github.com/pathofresonance/mpa-locals. Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both cause and effect features to determine an adjusted prediction function. This adjusted function mitigates the domain shift by being insensitive to the given causes. This approach is grounded in a new theoretical framework that generalized semi-supervised learning. We showcase the efficacy of our method using real-world datasets and compare its performance to other domain adaptation methods. Additionally, we provide a geometric intuition that might help explain the performance of our proposed approach. The code used to generate the results is publicly available. Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. Additionally, this geometric model facilitates the interpretation of inductive bias in deep learning systems. By examining the geometric structures of different neural networks, we obtain a collective understanding of the computational paradigms adopted by various deep learning architectures. Ultimately, this geometric model serves as a unified theoretical framework for the deep learning community to examine and compare the computational paradigms of different neural network architectures. To achieve this, the study uses a novel method, incorporating 'augmented' variables, known as XAUG variables, alongside standard input, then applies a layer-by-layer relevance analysis to both types of networks. XAUG variables are merged with intermediate network layers and utilised in final stages to interpret the classification outcome. Analysis shows XAUG variables enhance discrimination capabilities when combined with low-level features, in some instances capturing the classification entirely. This method, combined with the relevance analysis, allows researchers to determine crucial information networks rely on and identify essential features. In the study's findings, incorporating XAUG variables in deep neural networks enabled researchers to pinpoint key features and reduce the classification's reliance on irrelevant information. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. To validate our approach, we successfully calculate the equation of state for the attractive Hubbard model with up to 128 lattice sites and a moderate number of electrons. Our results demonstrate that the method retains the same level of accuracy as its predecessor, yet achieves substantial time savings, thereby facilitating extensive simulations of thermodynamic properties. Additionally, we showcase the capabilities of this method in a more complex scenario with the bosonic Hubbard model on a 64-site lattice, revealing a phase diagram with extensive reentrant superfluidity. Our analysis indicates that this method's efficiency will enable extensive scale-dependent studies of superfluidity and other complex quantum many-body systems. Furthermore, we recognize the potential for the method to be adapted and employed in a broader range of problems, such as quantum electrodynamics. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. We investigate several pretraining strategies for adding new languages and evaluate the models' performance on zero-shot language switching, translation tasks, and their ability to understand sentences in unfamiliar languages. The most effective method involves mixing unsupervised data from the new language with supervised data from other languages during pretraining, a technique found to significantly enhance zero-shot translation quality and facilitate understanding of sentences in the new language. However, this mixing does not substantially improve the models' performance on zero-shot language switching. We discovered that German, due to its significant grammatical differences, posed more challenges to adaptation compared to Korean. Notably, our research found that adapting the BigScience model to German took around 1-2 weeks using a NVIDIA A100 GPU, employing a batch size of 8. We further analyzed the models' behavior through various attribution methods and found that our results are consistent with prior research on multilingual adaptation, also reflecting some unexpected patterns, such as the reliance of German sentence embeddings on certain German words, being less understanding of others. We subsequently examined the potential for using adaptation on other languages, specifically by trying it on Zaz, an Iranian language with sparse online resources, and found that Korean, a language with completely different origins, could serve as an effective source for training. Ultimately, our study concludes that incorporating new languages into a large, multilingual model is feasible but may be hindered by existing knowledge of the established languages, requiring a mix of unsupervised and supervised data from the new language to achieve full understanding. We have made our code and data available for reproduction of our results. Additionally, we have established a GitHub repository for distributing the adapted models to the research community. We intend to expand our study to other languages, specifically by trying adaptation on German with Korean as a reference, and investigating the potential for using Japanese, a language with completely different origins, as a source for training. This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the Hybrid ICA approach ('hICA') effectively learns independent components in high-dimensional data through a decomposition-by-frequency method, its performance is hindered when dealing with large-scale datasets due to its reliance on generative models and multiple gradient descent iterations. In contrast, the FastICA algorithm is optimized for component extraction but is prone to component misidentification, which is particularly acute when dealing with small-dimensional data. To overcome these challenges, the m-ar-K-FastICA approach applies kernel-based methods to feature extraction and component identification, effectively reducing model complexity and mitigating the impact of local minima in optimization. By integrating the advantages of hICA and FastICA, the m-ar-K-FastICA approach enhances component identification while maintaining efficient optimization. In particular, this approach finalizes the component identification and extraction process after a specific number of iterations, thus bypassing the limitations associated with multiple gradient descent iterations. Our experimental results confirm that the m-ar-K-FastICA approach outperforms existing algorithms on simulated and real-world data sets. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/SahandR/m-ar-K-FastICA. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose NFND, a network-based framework for clustering related posts. Our evaluation shows that NFND can accurately distinguish between multiple narratives on a single topic and distinguish topic-specific narratives from those related to different topics. Furthermore, we provide two possible applications of NFND: a searchable knowledge base of social media-driven narratives and a system for detecting multiple narratives on social media. The latter application demonstrates the feasibility of NFND in a real-world setting and highlights potential areas for further development. Ultimately, NFND serves as a searchable platform for reconstructing social media debates and facilitating more structured discussions. The first component is a sentence embedding model for transforming sentences into numerical vectors, thereby enabling the comparison of sentences across different posts. The second component is a clustering algorithm for grouping the translated sentences into distinct narratives. We evaluated several embedding models and clustering algorithms to determine the most effective combination. The embedding models considered were: \textbf{TF-IDF}, a frequency-based model; \textbf{FastText}, a word vector model; \textbf{Universal Sentence Encoder (USE)}, an encoding model; and \textbf{DistilBert}, a transformer-based model. The clustering algorithms considered were: \textbf{DBSCAN}, a density-based algorithm; \textbf{K-means}, a partitioning algorithm; and \textbf{Leiden}, a community detection algorithm. The evaluation revealed that the combination of \textbf{DistilBert} and Leiden yielded the highest accuracy among the tested options. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our cumulative distribution function-based forecasting method, combined with incremental learning and adaptive sampling, provided more reliable and adaptable outcomes. Ultimately, we observed that our approach achieved superior accuracy in predicting a rumor's influence, facilitating more effective online rumor prediction and mitigation. The source code is available at https://github.com/amondbiao/COVIDRumor. This study was supported by NSFC/U1526206, 162602.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow. The full dataset and analysis code are available for reproduction on our GitHub repository. The RGit repository can be accessed at https://github.com/amir-arivani/Dimensionality-Reduction-on-Hyperspectral-Pixels. The Python package can be accessed at https://pypi.org/project/hrsr/. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. We will demonstrate through our experiments that a previously unattempted method of compressing language models, namely, transferring the parameters of a teacher network to a student network, can achieve compression ratios of up to 33.33 times with zero loss in accuracy, and even improve the model's performance in certain cases by up to 1.60 points. Our findings also show that the optimal compression approach depends significantly on the specific compression strategy employed, and therefore, a suitable model should be chosen based on the specific requirements of the task at hand. We also provide further evidence that supports the lottery ticket hypothesis and we identify the characteristics of the trainable sub-network. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits a thorough justification for the chosen loss function. This study seeks to examine how different loss functions impact performance across various datasets and model configurations. Our analysis involves evaluating eight diverse loss functions across six image classification datasets and three model architectures, revealing that certain loss functions can yield superior results but are rarely employed. We also uncover that no single loss function emerges as the optimal choice for a specific dataset, highlighting the need for greater guidance in selecting a loss function. Furthermore, our findings indicate that pre-trained models tend to perform better with certain loss functions, underscoring the importance of considering the base model when choosing a loss function. Finally, we observe that overparameterization can enable performance gains with less common loss functions, reducing the significance of a well-designed baseline model. Our code is publicly available on GitHub.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently ambiguous due to multiple possible interpretations. The present study adapts parquet theory to a description of particles in terms of fermions, applying it to the study of one fermion and two bosons interacting according to a specified potential, resulting in a set of three nonlinear equations that ensure the stability of the system and its conservation of properties such as momentum, energy, and symmetry. The emergence of additional terms in this description, not present in a perturbative description, is attributed to the inherent instability of pair-based interactions and is capable of supporting a stable solution at zero energy. The resulting theory is shown to be equivalent to a single equation derived from a description of the interacting system in terms of fermions and bosons, bound together in a complex entity known as a Dyson-Schwinger equation. The application of parquet theory at finite temperatures is also considered, capable of providing a description of particles that is consistent with experimental data. The resulting theory is shown to be a part of a larger class of theories that utilize nonlinear integral equations to describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently ambiguous due to multiple possible interpretations. The true potential of parquet theory, capable of describing the behaviors of the strong nuclear force, is also considered. In this context, the theory is shown to be a part of a larger class of theories, groundless in their current form but with a potential for future development and application. The development of a sensible parquet theory is contingent upon a deeper understanding of the scattering events that comprise it and is likely to be the key to unlocking a descriptive language for strong nuclear interactions. The study concludes by noting that while sensical applications of parquet theory may not yet exist, the theory's components, including the development of a sensible description of scattering events at all levels, is a promising area of continued research and development. The future of parquet theory may also be influenced by the development of new computational methods such as machine learning and neural networks, which could be utilized to develop a descriptive language for strong nuclear interactions. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed disparities in the emotional support provided by dispatchers across different organizations and incident categories. Notably, dispatchers who showed emotional support received higher response rates and faster responses from users. These results have provided significant knowledge to practitioners and system designers, inspiring the development of AI-powered tools to enhance human service quality. Ultimately, this work uncovers the hidden dynamics of human interactions within digital platforms. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The proposed approach is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/PlaidAI/MinimaxActiveLearning. The PyTorch implementation can be found at the established repository. It has been actively used by multiple research groups. The authors are willing to share the pre-trained models for benchmarking purposes. The team is open to collaboration and can be reached at p-rathore@umd.edu or prathore@umd.edu. We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D manifold. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is a specific type of manifold to the tune of $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, we identify a unique set of coordinates that capture the vortex loop's topological properties, effectively generalizing the concept of hyperelliptic function to singular vortices. A notable application of these results is the configuration space of a particle following a specific path, known as a billiard, within a bounded area. These findings also connect to other areas of mathematics, including moduli spaces and Teichmuller spaces. Moreover, we provide a detailed description of the group action on the Fock-Goncharov coordinates, establishing a connection between the configuration space and a specific type of manifold known as the moduli space of ribbon graphs. Finally, we propose a general approach to studying the motion of any singular vorticity type by establishing a connection between their orbit and the action of a specific group on the configuration space. This involves finding a suitable representation of the vorticity distribution, which can then be studied under the resulting group action. As such, this paper serves as a comprehensive introduction to the study of singular vorticity configurations. Various mathematical and physical aspects discussed herein were previously described in arXiv:2002.04354, arXiv:2006.09783, and arXiv:2010.15311. However, the connection between Fock-Goncharov coordinates and the hyperelliptic representation is specifically presented here for the first time. However, when using model-based predictions, incorporating them into ATE estimators leads to overfitting and biased estimates when compared to non-predictive models. To address this issue, we suggest normalized augmented inverse probability weighting (NAIPW), a method that uses the probability of treatment and outcome, adjusted for model residuals to eliminate overfitting when predicting treatment, and a weighted average of two IPW estimators for efficient use of data when including an additional model for the outcome, with boundary corrections. Through simulations and a case study on the application of antibiotics to treat pneumonia, the NAIPW method demonstrates improved bias and root mean square error when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the NAIPW method exhibits superior performance in model dependence and a high percentage of valid weights. Additionally, NAIPW can be applied to both model-based and non-predictive cases, with extensions to the double robust estimation approach and NAIPW's potential use in standardization. A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient estimation is achieved with minimal information loss. We also present a method for making predictions about future extreme events and evaluate this model, along with the proposed parameter estimation approach, using both simulated data and real-life loss datasets. Results demonstrate that this new estimation framework leads to more accurate predictions about future losses compared to traditional methods. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter than a day. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extreme environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Their analysis is based on transit data that were previously unexplored and includes new estimates of the planet's size and the distance between HD80606b and its star. As a result, the new study provides the most accurate description of HD80606b's orbit to date and confirms that the planet's size remains unchanged since its initial discovery. However, the new data do show a minor shift in the planet's position that suggests its orbit may be changing over time. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but typically do not discount outdated information.
As a result, memories become disorganized and the agent struggles to distinguish between relevant and irrelevant information.
To address this issue, we introduce MemoNav, a novel method utilizing a network called the Memory Selector to choose the most informative previous memories for navigation.
The memory selector leverages an iterative self-calibrated attention mechanism to selectively remember key moments and incorporate them into a unified goal representation.
By focusing on selective memories, MemoNav avoids misinformation and reduces noise, thereby outperforming existing methods on the ViATSN navigation benchmark. 
Additionally, we propose the Goal Clarity dataset, which provides goal representations to simulate varied levels of objective clarity for robustness evaluation.
Experimental results demonstrate MemoNav's effectiveness in navigating to objectives with as little as half the number of memories required by the top-performing previous method.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic aggregation in feature selection and test the performance of 1-D, 2-D, and 3-D convolutional neural networks on the challenging task.  To verify the proposed methods, a comprehensive database was established from recordings of various heart conditions, both with and without added noise, to ensure a diverse set of spectral patterns.  The results indicate that a specific neural network design, employing 1-D, 2-D, and 3-D convolutional layers in succession, yields a high accuracy of 88% in identifying abnormal heart sounds, even when they have been distorted by both types of noise.  Additionally, the proposed method demonstrates a high degree of robustness with a confidence interval of $\pm 2.5%.

In a discrete-time epidemic SISI model where population growth is constant and balanced, the per capita mortality and fertility rates are equivalent, and the model's evolution operator is a nonlinear function of seven parameters. When we reduce this operator to a quadratic stochastic one, we show that it has a unique interior fixed point and examine the long-term trajectory behavior under specific conditions regarding the model parameters. Furthermore, we numerically simulate the model under two different scenarios under which the transmission rates from infected to susceptible and from susceptible to infected individuals are altered in distinct ways. These scenarios yield intriguing patterns in the quantitative analysis of the model's trajectory equilibria. Additionally, we derive a family of critical lines separating regions of different long-term trajectory behaviors and find that the model exhibits complex dynamics, including periodic and chaotic behavior, when certain conditions are met. Finally, we propose two possible mechanisms for how these complex dynamics could arise in real epidemic SISI models. This work is a continuation of our earlier research on discrete-time epidemic SIS models featured in the Journal of Difference Equations and Applications, Volume 25, Issue 5. Unlike our previous research, where the evolution operator was a nonlinear function of five parameters, the present study involves a nonlinear function of seven parameters, reflecting real-world population characteristics such as age structure, where different age groups have distinct fertility rates. This study is a first attempt to explore the long-term trajectory behavior of discrete-time epidemic SIS models with population dynamics. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, we present MadDog, a free, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of analyzing texts input via its web interface or pasted into a text box. Utilizing a combination of machine learning and advanced algorithmic techniques, MadDog is designed to identify acronyms and determine their original meanings based on the context. Furthermore, users can review and manually correct the system's output through an interactive interface. We have also developed a dataset consisting of 792 acronyms across 42 domains. We anticipate MadDog to serve as a versatile tool for researchers and software developers seeking to integrate acronym identification into their existing projects or develop new applications, filling a long-standing gap in available solutions. Moreover, this dataset may be utilized for developing and refining acronym identification algorithms. Both the system and dataset are freely available at http://maddog.cl.isc.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/. We invite the research community to collaborate with us in further enhancing MadDog's accuracy across diverse domains. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the most notable manifestations of quantum physics. Historically, quantum interference has been observed in charge transport; however, recent findings indicate that it also significantly affects thermal properties. This insight enables the precise manipulation of heat within microscopic devices through phase-coherence. This study showcases how exploiting phase-coherent edge states in quantum Hall systems allows for the realization of exceptional thermoelectric properties and efficient heat rectification. A multi-quantum point contact tunneling setup with multiple interference paths was used to demonstrate that one can switch between heat generation and dissipation by adjusting electronic flux levels. Furthermore, a theoretical model was developed to show that this heat rectification system can function at a macroscopic scale and that its heat rectification ratio can be enhanced by increasing the tunneling strength. A thorough investigation of the system's thermoelectric properties and heat rectification capabilities through numerical simulations revealed that its heat conductance can be made highly asymmetric through interference-induced tunneling asymmetry. This property enables the realization of exceptional heat rectification and a thorough analysis of the system was provided using numerical simulations. This research paves the way for the development of compact thermoelectric devices and heat management systems. Additionally, this work is expected to broaden the understanding of the interconnected relationship between charge and heat transport in quantum Hall systems. Finally, this study lays the foundation for exploring other forms of heat rectification using quantum interference effects. Lastly, we examined the related physical phenomena occurring at quantum Hall junctions and found that they can be effectively described within a coherent framework. This research is expected to inspire further investigation into the complex relationships between these phenomena and their underlying microscopic mechanisms. It may also lead to new and innovative approaches to the development of artificial thermoelectric and heat management devices. Finally, this study demonstrates that quantum interference provides an ideal means of controlling charge and heat within microscopic systems and that its potential for shaping the future of quantum physics and engineering should not be underestimated. Additionally, we analyzed the related physical phenomena occurring at quantum Hall junctions and found that they can be effectively described within a coherent framework. This research is expected to broaden the understanding of the interconnected relationship between charge and heat transport in quantum Hall systems and may also lead to new and innovative approaches to the development of artificial thermoelectric and heat management devices.
