Our proposed DNA-storage system presents an innovative, compact representation of hierarchical data, exploiting the sequence relationship between DNA oligomers to streamline indexing and data revisions. Unlike existing solutions that treat DNA storage as regular storage, our system enables efficient management of hierarchical data and facilitates efficient data updates with the aid of short, synchronized oligomers, called "links." We introduce a new class of indices known as " hierarchy indexes" to optimize data indexing and revisions. By testing our solutions in a real-world scenario, our results demonstrate significant reductions in the size of indexed data and the number of writes required for revisions. For example, our findings show that when using a four-level hierarchy with four storage devices, our solutions result in a fourfold decrease in the size of indexed data and a significant 72% reduction in the number of writes required for revisions. We anticipate that these efficiencies will significantly enhance the performance of future large-scale hierarchical storage systems using DNA. In our evaluation, we introduce new metrics to gauge the practical value of our solutions in a real-world context. We also introduce a novel test, known as "oligomer alteration," to simulate errors in DNA storage and the effective solutions it reveals. Furthermore, our research identifies the link length as a crucial factor under consideration for any method aimed at supporting hierarchical data with DNA storage. We believe that our work will contribute substantively to the ongoing development of reliable and efficient DNA-storage technologies. We plan to make our implementation publicly available and to conduct further research in this area. We also propose an additional approach, "fusing links," that is grounded in a local exploration of oligomer sequences and links, and this approach is designed to provide even more efficient support for hierarchical data with DNA storage. In this approach, we aim to localize the effects of errors on the link sequence, and we propose an efficient algorithm to achieve this localization. We also present an indexing technique, "rerooting index," that is grounded in a general characterization of hierarchical data and "child and parent" functions, and this approach is designed to provide even more efficient support for hierarchical data with DNA storage. We demonstrate that these indices can be compactly represented and that they can be updated efficiently when revisions are needed. We show that "rerooting index" offers the most efficient support for hierarchical data, and we anticipate that this solution will significantly enhance the performance of future large-scale hierarchical storage systems. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the required level of specialization. This study presents an innovative approach to supplement a sparsely labeled collection of patient data by automatically extracting and incorporating ICD codes from a vast database of CTNs with established annotations. Through this semi-supervised method, the model's general performance and capacity to generate clinical text note labels as training data have been significantly enhanced. An experiment was conducted to compare the efficacy of this semi-supervised strategy with other existing techniques that rely solely on supervised training. The results of this comparison, using two distinct medical dataset combinations for evaluation, demonstrate that the semi-supervised approach consistently produces more accurate ICD codes compared to supervised training, specifically achieving an average 8.5% improvement in micro-F1 score across the two datasets. Additionally, the models trained through this semi-supervised strategy were found to be more resilient to data drift when handling new, unseen data. Further analysis of the model's decision-making processes revealed that its reliance on specific medical entities, such as body parts and symptoms, explains the success of this approach. Therefore, this semi-supervised strategy offers a promising solution for automatically generating clinical text note labels, potentially expanding the use of machine-learned ICD coding in practical, real-world clinical settings. The associated code for this research is publicly accessible via https://github.com/juliusfu/ctn-forecast. In addition, the pre-trained models and annotated datasets used in this study can be found at https://clinicaltextnotes.org/. A major breakthrough occurred when quantum mechanics was applied to machine learning, enhancing the ability to process larger datasets. However, the process of training a machine learning model on superconducting quantum devices is not well-defined. In this study, the authors present two quantum machine learning algorithms - a unsupervised learning component analysis and a supervised learning linear regression - that can be executed on superconducting quantum devices. They also experimentally implement these algorithms on an 8-qubit processor, achieving results equivalent to classical methods for small datasets. The study marks a significant step in advancing quantum machine learning and provides valuable insights for further research. An important finding of the study is that the phase transition in the unsupervised learning component analysis occurs at a point where the training and testing errors peak, a phenomenon observed in both quantum and classical computations. The study offers valuable lessons for designing circuits that can learn and the data for which they are suitable. A comparative study was also conducted to examine the relationship between training and testing errors in both quantum and classical linear regression models, and the findings revealed notable differences. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our proposed solution exhibits superior performance on a range of challenging datasets, including texture recovery, rigid pose estimation, and geometric deformation recovery. Additionally, we show that our differentiable renderer can be effectively used to generate training data for learning-based methods through self-supervision. Our renderer's code is available for public access at https://github.com/plg-uniwh/dsrenderer. Additionally, a demo application is available at https://dsrenderer.uniwh.pl.

Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs, with variations stemming from origin-destination demand, route choice, and unforeseen errors. By employing iterative least squares and lasso regularization techniques, the framework can iteratively estimate origin-destination demand while maintaining sparse covariance matrices for enhanced interpretability and computational efficiency. Notably, the probabilistic estimation method demonstrates an equivalent level of precision to the best possible estimators with diminishing errors as the sample size increases. The method was tested on two small-scale networks and two real-world large-scale networks, showing consistent and computationally efficient results with fast convergence. The study further confirms the effectiveness of lasso regularization in maintaining a balanced trade-off between the biases and variances of covariance matrix estimates. Furthermore, the study examines how varying origin-destination demand and route choice parameters affect the precision of origin-destination demand estimation, with route choice parameters showing a more pronounced impact than origin-destination demand parameters. The results also show that assuming a normal distribution for origin-destination demand does not significantly affect the iterative least squares estimator's convergence rate but results in marginally higher convergence rates compared to other distributions. Finally, the study highlights the applicability of the proposed framework in a real-world scenario involving signal control with the incorporation of day-to-day traffic data and origin-destination demand variables. The results show notable reductions in signal timing schemes and link flow, with considerable decreases in the probability of queueing and long queues as the sample size increases. The study's findings are expected to be useful for transportation system operators and the traffic management community. The proposed algorithm has been made available on GitHub for public access. The R code used to develop and test the methods is also available upon request from the author. The study's data and models can be obtained from TDA by submitting a request to the described agent. The study only utilizes publicly available data without involving human subjects. The mathematical expressions used in the study describe the behavior of statistical systems and can be derived from standard textbooks on probability theory and statistical inference. The study relies on standard methods and does not introduce novel algorithms or mathematical frameworks. The associated files provide a clear and detailed description of the study's methods and results

The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process. The outcome reveals the existence of a transition from stable global phases to localized waves mediated by a cusp catastrophe at the zero amplitude threshold. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. This research also proposes two possible enhancements to the hybrid method, aiming to enhance its performance and robustness. Ultimately, this study contributes a new, performance-oriented technique for generating uniform spanning trees and perhaps other random trees, leveraging the potential of combining random walks, as exemplified by the transient equivalence between Aldous-Broder and Wilson's algorithms. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances multimodal learning capabilities by offering a combined platform for sheet music, song lyrics, and musical audio. The dataset is designed to facilitate research across three main areas: music transcription, music audio generation, and multimodal learning. It consists of a substantial collection of 194,447 musical scores and associated audio files from the Mutopia Library and 84,651 song lyrics derived from the MetroLyrics website. To make the dataset even more useful, we have developed a set of tools and described several possible research applications. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth evaluation of various deep learning models using masked linear dependencies, masked attention, and supervision techniques to analyze their performance on music audio, sheet music, and song lyrics. The MusicTM-Dataset and accompanying code can be accessed through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/soudrymusicml/MusicTM-Dataset and imported into TensorFlow and PyTorch models for immediate use. Future updates to the dataset are planned to enhance its entitty enrichment capabilities. Keywords: MusicTM-Dataset, Music Audio, Sheet Music, Song Lyrics, Multimodal Learning, Music Transcription, Music Audio Generation.

Our research revealed that, in systems with pure cubic nonlinearity, we obtain a new stability criterion and prove stability for solitons with arbitrary phase. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach via a new coil set design that surpasses NCSX design goals, achieving a range of rotational transform targets from 0.3 to 0.6. Moreover, our design incorporates five distinct magnetic configurations, each with its own optimal rotational transform range. We found that optimizing coil sets for specific rotational transform ranges yields optimal results, surpassing a single optimal range design in volume preservation. Our novel design features integrates directly into the KFK code for efficient stellarator design manufacturing. We found that our design aligns with NCSX manufacturing constraints, with all essential coils located within the vacuum vessel volume. Future research will focus on further refining the design and evaluating quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume metrics in more detail. We anticipate this design approach will contribute to the development of more versatile stellarators. Speakers: C.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. The presented study's data has been made publicly accessible. Additionally, a customized 1D numerical model is provided that can be used to analyze the experimentally obtained temperature maps, thereby facilitating the identification of key heat transfer mechanisms and aiding the design of optimized catalyst packing arrangements for effective thermal performance. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. This new perspective on the Madsen-Weiss theorem highlights the deep connection between the theory of the b-principle and the advancements that have been achieved in the field of geometric topology. It also implies a new result known as the oriented colored broken submergence theorem, which asserts that any oriented colored broken submergence can be replaced by a oriented submergence in the underlying space of its compactification. This result will likely have significant applications in the field of geometric topology. It has been used to derive new proofs for a range of notable theorems, including Harer's stability theorem, Miller and Morita's work, and the standard Mumford Conjecture. It has also been applied to obtain new applications in the field of topological K-theory. These applications include the solution to a number of longstanding unsolved problems, and will be detailed in a separate paper. It is worth noting that the perspective offered in this note is limited to its connection to the field of geometric topology, and may not represent the full range of applications that the b-principle has to offer. The b-principle is a highly versatile theory, and is likely to have numerous other applications across a wide range of disciplines. In particular, it is believed that the theory may have significant connections to the field of quantum topology, and may have a number of other significant applications in the field. These potential applications are the subject of ongoing research, and will be detailed in a number of upcoming papers. It has also been applied to obtain new proofs for a number of notorious theorems, and will be detailed in a number of upcoming papers. The specific papers that detail these applications include, but are not limited to: A. Hatcher's and I. Koranyi's axiomatics for the theory of the b-principle, B. Harer's stability theorem, C. Miller and Morita's work, and D. the standard Mumford Conject

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A range of solution strategies employing Newton-Krylov solvers and different multigrid methods have been explored, with particular focus on the impact of grid size and domain complexity. Furthermore, by introducing "artificial complexity" through added degrees of freedom without changing the grid structure, researchers have simulated extreme domain complexities and analyzed the effects on multigrid preconditioning. Our study reveals that BDDC outperforms AMG for solving cardiac mechanics problems, with BDDC achieving up to two times faster convergence than AMG depending on the specific scenario. With the exception of one case where the convergence rates differ by a factor of 1.5, BDDC consistently offers superior performance compared to AMG. Moreover, as the size of the problem increases, the performance gap between BDDC and AMG also increases. Therefore, using BDDC for solving large-scale cardiac mechanics problems is the preferred approach. Additionally, this study identifies specific characteristics of the algebraic system that affect the convergence rate of BDDC and provides recommendations for improving the balance in the BDDC solver, thereby reducing its memory requirements and enhancing overall performance. Finally, this research provides code-level examples of how to implement the BDDC solver using the deal.II software library for the detailed methodology outlined in the paper. In particular, researchers have developed novel features, including an "extract subdomain" function, and demonstrated the balance analysis's role in determining the success of the BDDC solver. Furthermore, this study illustrates the performance of the BDDC solver when deployed in two distinct deal.II modules, in addition to offering guidance on the optimal implementation of the BDDC solver. In particular, researchers have identified the critical code level factors that contribute to the BDDC solver's performance and provided a comprehensive overview of the necessary deal.II features for running the BDDC solver, including an 'extract subdomain' function, for the specific heart mechanics problem. This has significant practical tailoring implications as researchers strive to enhance the BDDC solver's performance across various types of finite element grids and cardiac mechanics problems. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems supporting content creation and collaboration. Among these systems are tag-based platforms that facilitate shared annotation and discovery of content across communities. However, the success of such platforms heavily relies on several key factors including the sharing of tags among users and systems. This study examines characteristics of tag usage that enable their sharing and reapplication. It also explores how tags evolve over time within systems and how these dynamics contribute to the emergence of collaboration and shared interests. Our analysis focuses on Del.icio.us, a tag-based platform with a lifespan of nearly a decade, and reveals its growth into a complex network facilitated by both new and established users. It also reveals the existence of collaboration patterns evident in the shared annotation of content and the shared interests of users, and delves into the temporal dynamics underpinning these phenomena. Our work provides a framework for designing systems that facilitate collaboration, shared tasks, and shared interests by leveraging user-generated content. It also identifies challenges and bottlenecks within existing systems aimed at promoting these phenomena. Finally, our study contributes to the body of knowledge on the computational study of collaboration and shared tasks. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and a physical phenomenological model that accounts for thermoviscous effects. These designs can be fabricated using two-photon lithography and have been verified through both numerical simulation and experimental prototyping. Mobile IAB, which facilitates the connection of UEs in motion, holds potential as a suitable solution. This work takes a different approach from existing literature by providing a comprehensive overview of deploying mobile IAB by covering: the IAB standardization in 5G New Radio (NR); a classification framework for both fixed and mobile IAB; an extensive analysis of mobile IAB performance through simulations; and the open challenges and potential prospects of this technology. The proposed taxonomy organizes existing IAB research by categorizing different perspectives, while categorizing mobile IAB by the type of mobility involved. In terms of performance assessment, the authors analyzed mobile IAB deployments in urban environments, specifically buses to enhance passenger connectivity, which resulted in significantly improved throughput and energy efficiency compared to using fixed IAB. Nevertheless, mobile IAB was found to be susceptible to outages due to bus acceleration and deceleration, which may last for several hundred milliseconds. The authors explored these issues and the underlying physics of mobile IAB, which depend on factors such as bus speed, acceleration, and the backhaul loss rate. The open problems discussed include accounting for uncertainty in modeling traffic and backhaul losses, as well as the potential for using machine learning algorithms to address these challenges. I offer an alternative perspective on the transition from the wave equation to the Born rule. Instead of viewing the wave function as a fundamental description of nature, I present a case for seeing it as a probabilistic object derived from a more fundamental state function, essentially a wave equation. In this framework, I provide two types of justification for the Born rule - one based on simplicity and another on being 'physically consistent'. In the first case, I argue that the Born rule is the most basic form of a broader mathematical structure, essentially a measure theory with normalization constraints. By removing redundant variables, this perspective yields a fundamental probability density that can be easily calculated from a wave function. In contrast, alternative approaches like path integral quantization necessitate a more complex transformation. In the second case, I examine scenarios where measurements are not merely one-dimensional, effectively'reading' multi-dimensional wave functions as measurements. However, this gives rise to inconsistencies, addressing which leads to the Born rule as a solution. Although this approach has limitations and has already been tackled by more popular theories like path integral quantization, I make a case for its historical and physical significance. Finally, I propose a possible way to reconcile this perspective with other approaches to quantum theory. In a supplementary note, I explore a broader mathematical structure known as'spectral theory', revealing that both wave functions and probability densities belong to this structure, with the Born rule emerging naturally as a consequence. This approach, I believe, offers a fresh and interesting perspective on quantum theory. In a further supplementary note, I discuss the relationship between wave functions and probability densities from the viewpoint of 'distributions with support', revealing that the Born rule is not uniquely determined by this relationship, with further investigation required. This, I believe, presents an interesting research direction. In two more supplementary notes, I examine the distinction between rational and irrational wave function values from a historical and philosophical perspective, ultimately concluding that both paradigms have their rational and irrational roots. Furthermore, I reflect on how this distinction is reflected in the ongoing debate between realist and anti-realist interpretations of quantum theory. In another supplementary note, I consider the broader implications of this distinction for our understanding of space, particularly when it comes to measuring distances, with the wave function offering a useful framework for examination. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, tools are being developed that can mimic real-world learning scenarios. To contribute to this area of study, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), an open-source and comprehensive learning environment that simulates an experiential world where agents must navigate a 2D terrain to collect symbols, which are subsequently used to unlock new skills. The unlocking process represents the acquisition of new abilities, forcing the agent to adapt its strategy in light of its growing capabilities. L2Explorer is designed to test the ability of lifelong learning methods to effectively utilize previously acquired skills when encountering new tasks. The framework offers a range of flexible features, including adjustable L-D plots, multiple learning curves, and the ability to easily integrate new skills and evaluate the impact of various lifelong learning techniques. L2Explorer is made accessible under an MIT license and is available for public use at https://github.com/AttilaBenda/L2Explorer. We invite the research community to leverage this framework in their ongoing research. Additionally, a comprehensive study demonstrating its capabilities is also included in this document. We firmly believe that L2Explorer will become a valuable standard platform for ongoing and future research in the field of lifelong learning. Keywords: Lifelong Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Generalization, Exploration, Learning Curves, Open-source.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps with elliptical geometries that favor specific polarization modes. Due to anisotropic splitting in the cavity, ground state degeneracy is lifted, yielding fine structure modes along the trap's axis and orthogonal to it. These modes are selectively occupied by the condensate. Our results reveal a unique method for polarization control with potential applications in spin-based photonics and research on complex optical systems with adjustable coupling properties. Additionally, this technique could be applied to other systems with fine structure and can be adapted for widespread use in opto-spinics. A comparative study between coupled and single exciton-polariton condensates shows that coupling between condensates can lead to various complex states, but also allows for efficient transfer between states with compatible polarization. This transfer is enhanced when the coupling axis is aligned with the trap's axis, demonstrating the efficacy of our method in managing polarization. Ultimately, this research enables the development of controllable and coupled polariton condensate systems that could serve as a basis for complex photonic circuits. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables healthcare professionals to form more precise opinions. For retinal analysis in particular, recent advancements have led to increased use of multiple imaging methods: standard two-dimensional fundus photographs and more detailed three-dimensional imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography. Our study employed three distinct multimodal data fusion strategies centered on deep learning to tackle challenges in retinal analysis: early combination, intermediate fusion, and hierarchical integration. Noting that early and intermediate fusion approaches primarily serve practical purposes but struggle to adapt to varying data distributions, our team focused on developing a hierarchical solution. This project focused on fusion methods involving fundus photographs, OCT, and OCT angiography datasets from the public Stare and Drive databases. Our tests showed that an intermediate fusion strategy including two distinct image types yielded better results than the hierarchical approach. Building on this finding, we refined our approach to handle three-dimensional data by applying a more streamlined intermediate fusion strategy. Our work has potential applications in combining various medical imaging techniques and will likely influence future research in this area. Ultimately, our goal is to make diagnostic decisions more precise and effective through multimodal fusion. Our code is publicly available on our GitHub repository. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with significant predictive value for severe COVID-19 symptoms.  Identifying these features is essential for prioritizing critical care admission to save lives, given the limited capacity for mechanical ventilation.  Unfortunately, detecting these features is challenging due to their subtlety and the lack of visible symptoms in X-ray images, making it difficult to define a set of potential features.  To address this, we propose an automatic system to identify areas of lung infection and calculate features derived from infected lung area properties, such as area, density, and shape.  By leveraging these quantifiable features, we can develop models to predict severe symptoms and ICU admission with better accuracy.  Our proposed method was evaluated on the Berlin Dataset and demonstrated state-of-the-art performance, with promising results showing its potential to accurately identify severe COVID-19 cases using X-ray images.  Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of potential features related to ICU admission, featuring 21 quantities of lung region properties, thus contributing to the development of methods for detecting severe COVID-19 cases.  Our code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/AIforCOVID-20/PotentialFeatures.  We believe this work will facilitate the development of diagnostic systems for detecting severe COVID-19 cases by providing a precise specification of potential features derived from X-ray images.  It is anticipated that this work will be extended to address other medical image interpretation challenges.  From a technical standpoint, our method contributes to the tasks of lesion-synthesis and diagnosis, by limiting the range of detectable features to regions of lung infection.  We believe this targeted approach to feature detection will facilitate the development of diagnostic systems capable of accurately identifying severe COVID-19 cases. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. Furthermore, if the base category C has an initial object 0, then the simplicial groups (C,W) form a simplicial category that is algebraically coherent, and this coherence includes a universal property as described by Berman. The simplicial groups (C,W) also inherit various properties of the original universal bundle functor, including a homotopy theory that is compatible with monadic composition. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC for a particular measurement method does not exceed the trace norm of the difference between the measured density operator and the identity operator, with equality occurring in the case of projective measurements. Furthermore, the QCC for a specific weak measurement technique depends solely on the operator being measured and not on the post-measurement state, thereby serving as a characteristic function of that operator. Lastly, it's shown that the QCC for arbitrary POVMs (positive operator-valued measurements) can be achieved by employing a specific weak measurement technique. This leads to the realization that any quantum state with a QCC of zero must be expressed as a probability distribution over pure states. This research also offers a method for identifying quantum gates that perform projective measurements within any given quantum information processing scheme. This method may be adapted for identifying the gates associated with arbitrary POVMs as well. Additionally, a potential application of the concept of QCC is explored in the context of device-independent quantum key distribution. Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an input image. This network, called the Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN), utilizes GRUs to iteratively refine social connection representations by combining visual, semantic, and attribute information. By employing attention mechanisms, the network is enabled to focus on relevant elements. Additionally, the network is trained using a balanced sampling method to counteract the sparsity of social relationship data. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this end-to-end system. The accompanying supplementary material contains further information. The end-to-end system is comprised of image preprocessors, a balanced sampling method, and the GRG-GN, which iteratively generates social relationship graphs, as well as a detailed analysis of our study. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/ozanozuhr/SRG-GN. This research is a development of previous work in social relationship recognition, and is an extension of the findings reported in Liu et al. (2018), with code released at https://github.com/zhengwei-liu/SRRC. The underlying dataset utilized for training and testing the network is called the Social Relationship dataset. It consists of 20,008 images, derived from the Residual Image Network, with a varying number of objects and attributes. The dataset is designed to test a system's ability to understand diverse social interactions. The accompanying supplementary material contains additional information on the Residual Image Network. The Residual Image Network was developed to address the challenge of object omission, and is comprised of a pair of reciprocal networks. When the first network is fed a complete image, it produces a reduced output, and when fed a reduced output, it strives to recreate the original complete image. Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone that outperforms state-of-the-art models in image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, while using significantly fewer resources and parameters. The code and models will be publicly available. The authors also conducted extensive ablation studies to confirm the efficacy of their approach. The dynamic graph message passing network was found to effectively model long-range relationships by passing messages across multiple graph scales and performing global re-attention for superior performance. For instance, a simple global re-attention approach led to a 7.5% improvement over a state-of-the-art semantic segmentation model on the test area50-folds dataset. The dynamic graph message passing network was also found to have similar semantic message passing patterns as a pre-trained Transformer backbone, which indicated the effectiveness of the local attention filter and the global re-attention mechanism in the graph neural network. Moreover, the study found that the dynamic graph neural network had efficient semantic sparsity and graph sparsity properties due to the local attention filter and the global re-attention mechanism, which led to a 5.2 times reduction in the number of graph messages passed compared to a pre-trained Transformer backbone. The study also conducted further analyses on the graph structure, the graph neural network, and the local attention filter to understand the underlying components of the dynamic graph message passing network. The researchers also demonstrated the performance of the dynamic graph message passing network on other computer vision tasks, such as pose estimation and scene parsing, and found that it led to a 9% improvement over state-of-the-art models on the pose estimation task with much reduced computational cost. The paper also presents a detailed study on the design of the dynamic graph message passing network, including an in-depth analysis of the choice of head, the scale of the graph, the message passing process, the local attention filter, and the global re-attention mechanism. The researchers conducted an ablation study on the graph neural network to confirm the efficacy of the dynamic graph message passing

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. The optimal constant values, however, depend on the specific circuit specifications which are difficult to optimize directly. Existing approaches often rely on heuristic techniques that don't guarantee the best possible hardware efficiency. In this study, we establish a mathematical framework to find the best constant values for MCM operations based on hardware cost, but this is proven to be an NP-complete problem. We then present an iterative optimization algorithm and experimental results showing its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions compared to previous methods. The source code of this study is available at https://github.com/jaakkoheinonen/MCM-OPT. The experimental results are publicly available on GitHub. High-definition hyperspectral images possess the unique capability to distinguish between diverse objects within intricate environments by analyzing each pixel across various frequency ranges. Although HSI cameras are becoming increasingly accessible, associated algorithms have not been extensively utilized. This research delves into a novel application, specifically employing hyperspectral images for cityscape object segmentation using an unsupervised learning approach that circumvents the need for manual object classification. This method capitalizes on the rich spectral data inherent in HSI images, allowing for the efficient segmentation of cityscapes without requiring manual object classification. By analyzing the inherent properties of HSI images and developing a corresponding classification framework, we demonstrate how these images can be used to improve object segmentation in complex city environments. This technique offers a viable alternative to traditional approaches and can be used as a cost-effective solution for object extraction in cityscapes. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method is competitive with object extraction algorithms that rely on more sophisticated multi-modal data, including domain adaptation and deep learning-based approaches. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a puzzle. Possible explanations for its unique internal rotation profile include the star's encounter with a nearby companion that caused desorption of light elements or the star's interaction with a planetary body that resulted in diffusion of elements and altered its structure. Additionally, this star's unusual characteristics may be attributed to angular momentum redistribution within it, induced by mechanisms other than traditional tidal interactions. Further observations, as well as seismic data, are required to clarify the star's internal composition and the causes of its distinctive rotation characteristics. If confirmed, this star can serve as a valuable comparison to the asteroseismology of solar-like stars, providing insight into its evolution and the processes that shaped it. Additionally, this star's characteristics can be utilized to illustrate the potential of solar-like stars to engulf planets. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite being widely adopted, the RAM model lacks a solid theoretical foundation, characterized by inconsistent definitions and a lack of cohesive results. This research aims to rectify this issue by developing a new RAM model with added layer and obtaining a complementary function set to obtain constant-time arithmetic operations with a linear-time algorithm. Furthermore, we prove essential bounds for the number of required shift operations, exploiting recent advances in testing circuit identity via the RAM model. Additionally, we demonstrate that any algorithm designed for a specific set of functions can be adapted for the base set alone within a constant number of layers. We believe this foundation will facilitate meaningful discussions about algorithm complexity. We also provide a simple example to illustrate the significant difference between algorithm complexity and machine complexity. Finally, we suggest that investigating the complexity of finding rectangular arrays with specific integer entries might be an intriguing area of exploration. Overall, this research seeks to rectify the inconsistent definitions and layer complexities of algorithmic complexity to establish a solid theoretical foundation. As such, some results may seem straightforward or even obvious, but they are crucial for establishing a cohesive and cohesive results. We hope this research will serve as a starting point for others to build upon. We have attempted to make the presentation as accessible as possible, assuming only basic knowledge in algorithms and RAM model. We have included extensive proofs, which might otherwise be typical in a corresponding journal article but are omitted here to streamline the presentation. We have included two appendices, one containing the proof of a crucial lemma and another providing additional results that might be of interest. We have also included two brief overview sections, one summarizing the research and presenting an intriguing problem, and another providing an accessible introduction to the RAM model. We have made sure to include all necessary references to provide a self-contained presentation. We hope this research will be useful to the scientific community. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. Our integrals have further application in identifying non-zero homology classes in the graph complex, providing novel perspectives on the cohomology and homology of the general linear group. In particular, homology and cohomology classes exist if and only if the corresponding graphs are not strictly collapsible. We propose a further conjecture: a graph is non-collapsible if and only if it features no collapsing chains of three or four edges. In support, we present a simple algorithm to determine whether a graph can be collapsed. Our method has associated advantages: it relies on explicit geometric analysis and simple graph topology principles, rather than the use of moduli space techniques and the analysis of feynman integrals. In particular, the period integrals of differential forms are expressible as finite sums of integrals over metrics, rather than infinite volumes. We provide a detailed, explicitly-computed example for the period integral of a specific invariant differential form on a specific graph. The computation relies on an interpretation of the form as a sum of weighted, discrete invariant differential forms on the graph's subgraphs. The weights are specifically structured so as to facilitate computation by reduction to the previously-introduced generalised feynman integrals. The same approach can be applied to other invariant differential forms, allowing for their integrals to be computed. In particular, we assert but do not prove a further result: the period integrals of all first cohomology classes of the general linear group are expressible as generalised feynman integrals. We propose a further set of conjectures on the relationship between graph collapsibility and the vanishing of invariant differential forms, providing the integration of which would yield feyman integrals. This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, this finding is consistent with the category-orthogonal object features theory, which suggests that effective object categorization depends on identifying both relevant and irrelevant object features that are stable across different categories but vary between objects.  Our results demonstrate that such features are indeed passed on through recurrence and facilitate superior object categorization performance.  This research provides the first empirical evidence supporting the category-orthogonal object features hypothesis and reveals the specific information processing mechanisms underlying successful object categorization in clutered environments. Finally, this study highlights the significance of including auxiliary variables in internal representations for object categorization, presenting potential implications for object manipulation and other motor tasks that require accurate extraction of object features. We also investigated the properties of an extended Hatano-Nelson chain, which demonstrates substantial correlation effects; interactions abolish the skin effect that exists in the non-interacting system. The findings of this study underscore the instability of the skin effect against correlations, which is consistent with the reduced point-gap topology in one spatial dimension. The discoveries presented here provide novel insights into the topological characteristics of correlated systems, thereby initiating new areas of research within the field of non-Hermitian topological physics. In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.

The distinct nature of the valleys in silicon, characterized by distinct orientations relative to the lattice, gives rise to a patterned interference pattern.
This unique property, combined with the capacity to control the positions of dopants with precision, provides a means to study the valley degree of freedom and associated entanglement in silicon. 
In this study, distinct varieties of donor states also gave rise to distinct interference patterns, and the relative contributions of Coulomb interactions and tunneling were systematically adjusted, leading to distinct interpretations based on whether valley states are entangled or remain distinct. 
This distinction, though based on different models, does however share a connection with a more general theory, known as many-body Landau theory. 
A particular case, where valley entanglement is broken but spin entanglement remains intact, was also studied and contrasted with a hypothetical scenario where valley states are securely coupled but individual spins remain distinct. 
Finally, a means to distinguish between these two scenarios has been proposed, involving the use of magnetic field to disentangle spins, thus determining whether valley states are securely coupled or individual spins are, in fact, distinctly positioned.

Given an algebraic variety X that has a transitive action from the group Aut(X), the highest degree of transitivity of this action is called the transitivity degree. This degree is denoted by the maximum value of m for which Aut(X) acts transitively m times on X. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems and conjectures. Notably, a quasi-affine toric variety has a transitivity degree of infinite if and only if it is toric and non-degenerate. For m = 2, the transitivity degree can be determined by examining the toric divisorial ideals of the variety. These ideals are also used to investigate whether the action of Aut(X) is 2-transitive on the set of its non-singular subvarieties. Moreover, the study involves computing the transitivity degree for specific spaces, such as the variety of 2n+1 matrices of rank at most r, and the variety of linear self-map pairs whose product has determinant d. A linear self-map pair is defined as a pair of linear maps between finite dimensional vector spaces over a finite field. The study also examines the connected component group of the variety of linear self-map pairs whose product has determinant d, and investigates the transitivity degree for specific actions related to this group. Notably, a linear self-map pair action is 2-transitive if and only if the connected component group has a non-zero element with the property that the determinant of the pair's product is d. Our approach recognizes that for multi-particle states, the total system momentum is the only well-defined property. Calculating the total momentum involves non-commutative composition of individual particle momenta, which become ambiguous. Our results indicate that previous Fock space constructions were flawed due to incorrect assumptions and lack success. We demonstrate that momentum exchange underlies a relativistic covariance principle in the braiding of quantum numbers, solving a persistent challenge in the field. This solution unveils a novel understanding of quantum number interactions and lays the groundwork for developing a consistent Fock space and scattering theory. Moreover, our framework reveals that the interaction of particles is an inherent feature of non-commutative space-time, making it impossible to isolate individual particles. Finally, we show that our theory is compatible with the requirement of causally separated observables and that the vacuum state is stable under renormalization. We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors. We utilize this technique to
investigate charge transport in scCVD diamond by exciting its charge carriers
with a femtosecond laser. We report results obtained from diamonds grown by
CVD method, which show three-dimensional charge transport patterns. Our data
surveys charge carrier mobility across an 80 micrometers diameter area and
at varying levels of excitation density. We observed that charge carriers are
confined to specific regions of the diamond crystal structure and that their
movement is impeded by certain obstacles. These difficulties originate from
diamond crystal lattice irregularities and result in the separation of the diamond
into different charge transport regions. We studied these regions and determined
their mobility, density, and distribution across an 80 micrometers diameter area
and at different levels of excitation. These findings could greatly benefit the
development of diamond-based high-power quantum electronics. (Author) |

Social media platforms are facing significant problems due to the presence of toxic content like hate speech, off-color language, and misogyny. These difficulties have caught the attention of the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community, driving innovative research in the field. In this study, we report on the performance of our models in the inaugural Arabic Misogyny Identification challenge, where we evaluate three models that can learn multiple tasks simultaneously, alongside their individual-task counterparts. Our approach relies on the pre-trained MARBERT language model to analyze text inputs. Our results indicate that the proposed models achieved top-tier outcomes, securing first, second, and third place in both the misogyny identification and classification tasks. Notably, our top-performing model achieved an F1 score of 70.6% in the classification task. These successes are followed by a detailed explanation of the models, along with an analysis of the challenges encountered during data processing. Our code is available for review on our GitHub repository. (https://github.com/ebrahimi-ws/Misogyny Identification)

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Building upon the concept from PILCO, a method for probabilistic policy search, our research demonstrates that constraining the uncertainty in the Gaussian Process model's dynamics has a beneficial effect on policy updates and results in more resilient controllers. In addition, our findings highlight the practical advantages of this approach in a simulation-based evaluation. Notably, our modifications to PILCO's framework also enable faster convergence and increased transfer learning capabilities. In comparison to related methods for robust policy search, like MAME and GP-BayesNet, our developments result in controllers with superior performance and adaptability. The benefits of constraining uncertainty are further illustrated in a study of a 7 DoF robot's flexible joint control system. The findings of our research suggest that controller robustness can be directly affected by the system's dynamics and that discovering and minimizing unstable modes is essential for optimal policy search. Several key network communication challenges such as caching and computation are interconnected. A centralized caching approach seeks to mitigate network strain during peak wireless network times, while a distributed computation approach aims to minimize strain in data transfer between storage and reception devices. This paper, drawing inspiration from a study of these schemes, reveals a previously overlooked connection between caching and computation schemes. This connection enables the adaptation of a variety of established caching schemes for use in computation, and vice versa. A unified model is introduced for this new relationship, and it is shown that schemes involving linear combinations of packets can be easily transformed into each other. Furthermore, it is proven that any effective caching scheme can be converted into an effective computation scheme, and vice versa, when applying a linear encoding approach. This new understanding has the potential to broaden the scope of study in these areas and facilitate the design of new schemes. Additionally, it is proven that any caching scheme can be converted into an index coding scheme, which is a special type of caching scheme. Established caching schemes such as centralized caching schemes with zero, one, and multi-rounds; distributed caching schemes such as fully distributed, two-layer, and multi-layer schemes; and a hybrid caching scheme are shown to be equivalent to specific computation schemes. Furthermore, a new family of caching schemes, known as distributed caching schemes with sigma products, is developed and proven to be effective. It is also shown that the optimal file transfer rate in a single-round centralized caching scheme is 2/3, and a new quantization approach is proposed to reduce the data transfer volume in a multi-round centralized caching scheme by a factor of approximately 0.39. Finally, a new distributed computation scheme is proposed that requires only 11 data transfers, and it is proven to be 5 times more efficient than the current best known scheme requiring 55 data transfers. The same approach is also applied to a hybrid caching scheme and a specific computation scheme known as the compute-and-forward framework, and it is shown that any effective caching scheme can be converted into an effective compute-and-forward scheme, and vice versa, when applying a linear encoding approach. The proposed computation scheme is further tested and shown to be superior to other known schemes in various scenarios. Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability. The findings suggest that the addition of geometric constraints results in more precise collision avoidance, factoring in the robot's spatial structure. Moreover, the increase in parameters' nonlinearity does not affect the method's efficiency. The developed strategy's adaptability and ease of integration with geometric constraints make it a vital tool for designing efficient collision avoidance systems. Polynomial system solving plays a crucial role in various applications to capture nonlinear geometric attributes. To obtain a solution set devoid of degeneration, which end-users seek to avoid, the nondegenerate locus of a polynomial system needs to be computed. The nondegenerate locus comprises solutions where no codimension-one degeneration occurs. Calculating it poses a challenge for general solving methods, which are rewritten to incorporate the nondegenerate condition through an embedded dynamic elimination process. A signature-based algorithm is then developed to efficiently determine if a nondegenerate point qualifies for a solution, which it does by examining specific coefficients known as signatures. As a result, the algorithm avoids complicated dynamic elimination in favor of an alternative approach that directly evaluates these signatures. If a point satisfies this condition, it is confirmed as a solution, otherwise the algorithm proceeds with a modified version of the dynamic elimination process. The algorithm demonstrates a mechanism to bypass costly dynamic elimination in favor of an alternative approach that directly evaluates these signatures. The algorithm showcases a new strategy using these signatures to determine relevant solution properties, which it achieves by examining these signatures, thereby capitalizing on their computational value. Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of the 200 GeV Cu$+$Cu collisions. By calculating the $e^{+}e^{-}$ excess in the $e^{+}e^{-}$ mass distribution over hadronic contributions, we found that quasi-real direct virtual photons significantly contribute to the photon spectrum. In Cu$+$Cu collisions, photons show an excess over p$+$p measurements, particularly at lower $p_T$ values, hinting at a possible influence of hot and cold nuclear matter effects. In contrast, we found no $A$-$P_T$ dependence for direct photons in Cu$+$Cu events. Moreover, we determined the inverse slopes of the direct photon spectrum and $e^+e^-$ excess as functions of $N_{\rm coll}$ and established their similarity in form, especially for $s_{_{NN}}$=200 GeV collisions. Finally, we noted that quasi-real direct virtual photons account for approximately two-thirds of total direct photons in Cu$+$Cu events and suggested that their photon spectrum behavior follows a similar power-law pattern with hadronic components as their $e^+e^-$ excess follows a similar temperature dependence. In summary, we have successfully disentangled direct photons from hadronic contributions in Cu$+$Cu collisions and obtained valuable insights into their properties within a single collision event. This work implies direct photons can serve as a unique probe for assessing partonic phase properties in heavy-ion collisions. In doing so, we have developed a novel and crucial observation: the partonic phase in Cu$+$Cu collisions at $N_{\rm coll}$=20 per unit area exhibits the same temperature and density characteristics as that found in Au$+$Au collisions at $N_{\rm coll}$=20. Furthermore, we noted that quasi-real direct virtual photons may also be prevalent in other systems such as proton-$+$proton collisions and proton-$+$lead collisions at LHC energies, thereby potentially broadening direct photon's utility in exploring partonic phase properties in a variety of systems. This research may also facilitate data reanalysis in Au$+$Au and proton-$+$proton systems to better comprehend partonic phase behavior. The codegree squared sum, or co2(G), is introduced to measure codegree magnitude in a 3-uniform hypergraph, with exco2(n,H) representing the maximal codegree squared sum among n-vertex H-free hypergraphs. Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In response to these challenges, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance point rendering pipeline based on the GPU's primitive processing capability. The proposed technique efficiently generates anti-aliased line joins on vector maps by leveraging the GPU's primitive sorting capability, eliminating the need for complex vertex shaders and triangle fan or line strip rendering. As a result, this approach significantly reduces the size of the program binary and yields exceptional frame rates in line join rendering. Furthermore, this technique's minimal memory footprint enables the distribution of the program binary across various platforms. Our findings demonstrate the substantial advantages of this solution, where it outperforms existing line join rendering techniques both in terms of visual quality and system performance. Specifically, the technique achieves a 56.9% increase in program binary size efficiency and a 30.7% boost in rendering efficiency, ultimately leading to a 34.9% decrease in frame rate error. In practical terms, this means that on a standard Android 10 device, the program binary size associated with our technique amounts to 2.24 MB, whereas the line join rendering efficiency reaches 1577 fps. These substantial improvements will certainly facilitate the efficient rendering line joins on vector maps on diverse devices. On the basis of this innovative rendering pipeline, we also devise two anti-aliased line join rendering techniques that produce a self-intersecting cap, yielding a cap color based on the pixel coverage of the cap. By employing this straightforward mechanism, the line join appears continuous and the cap color is determined accurately. To achieve an optimal visible cap, we introduce a cap rectification mechanism that effectively eliminates the width of the line join and generates a visible cap. Moreover, to solve the triangle fan and line strip rendering issue and achieve a rounded cap, we devise a point rendering pipeline based on triangle rendering, where we control the color of the cap by adjusting the pixel coverage of the cap. Ultimately, this approach significantly reduces the size of the program binary and yields exceptional line join rendering performance on various devices. As proof of concept, the technique has been implemented and demonstrated on Google Map. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency. As an alternative, we also suggest a piecewise linear interpolation method based on the same RBF that maintains the original scheme's characteristics, even when using transcendental values. Notably, these methods outperform previously established schemes in terms of convergence rate. The article includes appendices containing additional proof and scheme specifications. It is also accompanied by a code file demonstrating the application of these methods to 2D and 3D test functions. The corresponding software is available at https://github.com/jacopoandrea/LSRBIP. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus supporting theoretical models predicting reduced diffusion within localized areas near pulsar wind nebulae. It is hypothesized that the significant decrease in diffusion is likely due to the presence of strong magnetic fields, thereby influencing cosmic ray behavior and potentially resolving the outstanding puzzle of minimal cosmic ray detection on Earth. This article discusses the established pulsar halos and provides a comprehensive review of the relevant research, including theoretical predictions and observational findings. It also considers the diffusion properties of pulsar halos, the global distribution of pulsar halos, and the associated cosmic ray leakage. Finally, the article explores the minimal diffusion out of the Galaxy and its implications on understanding cosmic ray propagation. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of relevant data.
Existing datasets are also incomplete, containing images of only three weather conditions: snow, rain, and clear skies.
To address this, we introduce the WeatherSeg dataset, consisting of 20 unique weather types identified through the analysis of images.
The dataset is tailored for segmentation tasks and can be applied to develop a real-time weather detection system.
Moreover, we share our findings on the effectiveness of data augmentation in the weather detection context.
Assessing several Convolutional Neural Network approaches on the WeatherSeg dataset, we found that a Deep Convolutional Network trained on augmented data performed better than other methods.
Our study also compares the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks on the WeatherSeg dataset with that on other prominent datasets, showcasing our approach with a notable 25% higher IoU and 2.8% higher accuracy. The source code of our project is available at https://github.com/fatemehkarimii/WeatherSeg.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Moreover, our analysis finds that science journals and policymakers tend to follow the lead of other groups, including scientists, economists and the general public, in terms of their attention to climate change. Furthermore, we find that the transition to a more prominent climate change policy is influenced not only by economic considerations but also by science and social norms. In sum, our findings underscore the significance of considering multiple drivers of climate change policy along with economic factors, as well as the value of timely policy action. On a broader note, our research highlights the utility of analyzing the co-evolution of social norms among different groups through a systematic and data-driven approach. By doing so, it may be possible to develop more effective strategies for addressing environmental concerns that are embedded in broader social dynamics. Finally, as one implication of our research, we suggest that policymakers could draw inspiration from the work of climate economists, as well as from each other and from scientists, in terms of their advocacy for a more prominent role for climate change. Similarly, scientists could learn from one another, as well as from each other and from economists, in terms of their communication of the need for action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In sum, our research indicates that there is value in "talking across" groups and suggests various avenues for such cross-fertilization. In a related vein, we believe that our analytical approach, which is centered on the co-evolution of social norms, could be applied to many other domains in addition to climate change. In fact, we see our research as just the first step in a broader program of inquiry that could ultimately lead to a more nuanced understanding of the complex interconnections among the various drivers of climate change policy and to more effective strategies for addressing the related "tragedy of the commons." In this sense, our research is presented as a series of preliminary findings rather than a definitive outcome.
