Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, current methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time applications. In this research, we propose an online algorithm that uses the Koopman operator theory to update and refine a dynamic model in real-time, even when the model itself is highly non-linear and infinite-dimensional. By integrating the updated model into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) structure, our approach enhances the control structure as well. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach by successfully adapting it to control multi-fingered soft grippers in simulation and in real-world experiments. The experimental results show a notable improvement in the grip success rate, with the online model and control method achieving results comparable to those of carefully optimized off-line models. The integration of this approach with existing estimation and sensing technologies has the potential to significantly expand the use of soft grippers in practical applications. Additionally, our method contributes to the development of model-free or learned control methods that could be crucial for efficiently using the sensors and estimation algorithms necessary for deploying artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) applications on physical systems. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effective results. However, this method's simplicity comes with a significant assumption: it only works when the function's gradient is correctly calculated. If the gradient is offset in any direction, the method may diverge. To address this limitation, a new method is proposed to solve optimization problems in an unbiased manner. To achieve this, the natural base manifold is employed, allowing the method to generalize Gradient Descent. A set of natural gradient descent equations is derived and proven to converge to the optimal solution under certain conditions. To simplify the complexity of finding the natural gradient, an iterative algorithm is proposed, demonstrating how each iteration can be completed analytically. The method is then tested on three real-world problems: reducing a complex function, identifying the parameters of a complex dataset, and controlling a complex robot movement, showing better results than Gradient Descent in reducing the cost more efficiently. The source code is available at https://github.com/ojello/GNGD. The primary contribution of this work is generalizing Gradient Descent to an unbiased numerical optimization method. By iterating on the natural gradient in the correct direction, the method is proven to converge to the optimal solution. The proposed algorithm can be applied to various problems in science and engineering, as demonstrated by successfully testing it on reducing a complex function, identifying the parameters of a complex dataset, and controlling a complex robot movement. The method is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ojello/GNGD. Future work will involve further generalizing the method to allow for multiple variables and exploring its application to the solution of partial differential equations. The method shows promise in providing a reliable and efficient solution to optimization problems, potentially replacing Gradient Descent in many applications. The use of the natural base manifold allows for an unbiased numerical optimization approach, surpassing the limitations of Gradient Descent in finding the lowest cost value for a given function. The proposed algorithm can be used to improve various methods by providing a reliable and efficient solution to optimization problems. The test on reducing a complex function in one dimension is successful, proving the method's capabilities. The failure to converge in the noisy test demonstrates the method's reliance on good quality data. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole's early history.  By studying the evolution of its surrounding plasma, one can get a glimpse into the black hole's early history.  A nearby, weak emission from a young radio source called J2102+6015 has been discovered using the e-MERLIN array.  This discovery, made possible by high-resolution images, has revealed two distinct sources - the initially thought-to-be-single source is now shown to consist of two separate objects.  One source, confirmed through a detailed spectrum, is a highly energetic source called J2102+6015 with a massive black hole, sitting at a distance of approximately 10 billion light-years.  J2102+6015 is notable for its high emission, strong magnetic force, and rapid rotation, and is now considered to be one of the youngest known radio source with a massive black hole, existing for a relatively short period of time.  Scientists think that J2102+6015 may be in a transitional phase, and further research using high-resolution imaging is needed to confirm its current state and future developments.  J2102+6015, along with other ancient radio sources, challenges the existing theory that supermassive black holes initially go through a highly energetic "quasar" phase before switching to a less energetic "black hole" phase, and further research using high-resolution imaging is needed to confirm its current state and future developments. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predictive accuracy using a dataset from 422 non-small cell lung cancer patients. Moreover, the study validates the feasibility of predicting survival times in subgroups defined by important genetic markers, thereby enhancing patient care and outcomes. The findings and methodology of this study have been made available on the CancerProSE GitHub repository for further investigation. The model's prognostic predictions are also accessible through a web-based CancerProSE Predictor. This research aims to bridge the gap between current prognostic models and actual doctor-patient interactions, enabling more effective medical strategies and, ultimately, better quality of life for lung cancer patients. The study's ethical considerations are discussed in detail. The integration of medical images and text data, along with the proposed model, were key to achieving accurate survival time predictions. The model's code and data can be accessed via CancerProSE at https://cancerprose.github.io/. A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies. We also introduce three datasets: Trajectory-Parallel Training, Interactive Storytelling, and Financial Conversation navigation, which offer novel challenges and opportunities for research in natural language state representation. We expect this overview to serve as a valuable resource for researchers seeking to tackle similar problems and navigate existing literature. The associated repository includes 17 implemented methods and 4 datasets for reproducibility and future reference. We hope this overview will foster innovation in the area, enabling researchers to develop novel natural language state representation methods. We also aim to bridge the gap between Reinforcement Learning and natural language processing, which has historically been distinct, with applications in areas such as clinical practices, video games, and human-robot interaction. As an example of the potential applications of these techniques, we have developed an Interactive Financial Guidance system, which assists users in achieving their navigation goals through natural language conversations. A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities. The approach's code is publicly available at https://github.com/edwindeleon-s/matter_reconstruction_with_ml. In addition, the corresponding dataset can be accessed through https://doi.org/10.6084/m1eissn.101.92171.

These models can predict matter density power spectra with an error rate of approximately 1%. We investigated the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, providing valuable insights that will facilitate analysis of forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities. This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish the characteristics of modules whose restrictions to $U(\frak h)$ are one-dimensional over Lie algebras representing differential operators on a circle. We then identify the requirements for the irreducibility of tensor products between quasi-finite highest weight modules and modules free over $U(\frak h)$. Additionally, we show that these tensor products are isomorphic only if their corresponding base modules are equivalent, before expanding our findings to cover general Lie algebras representing differential operators. Lastly, we outline a problem concerning the module complex formed by raising the tensor power of a one-dimensional module to an odd power and its relationship with the composition factor spectrum of quasi-finite highest weight modules. This problem has implications for understanding the structure of the composition factor spectrum of any quasi-finite highest weight module. The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). We found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion and established a formula to calculate the power spectral density of SGWMB, assuming that binary black hole mergers follow a Poisson distribution uniformly occurring across space and time. The strength of SGWMB is comparable to the usual gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes. The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate interest from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this attention lies in the word prediction challenge, where given a sequence of words in a sentence, a model is tasked with recommending the subsequent word. Researchers have addressed this issue through various techniques, combining either syntactic or semantic analysis methods in the past. However, individually, these approaches often fail to yield practical results in real-world applications. For instance, latent semantic analysis can capture semantic text characteristics, but it disregards syntactic constraints when generating word suggestions. In contrast, more advanced models like Deep Learning integrate both methods to achieve impressive outcomes. While these models can be computationally demanding, hindering their feasibility in certain scenarios, continuous advancements in technology and mathematical modeling enable the development of faster and more effective systems. A hybrid word suggestion model proposed here, combining elements of Naive Bayes and latent semantic analysis and considering context provided by surrounding words in the sentence, demonstrates considerable improvement over previous models. Furthermore, this model, when implemented using modern mathematical techniques like tensor computation, exhibits high efficiency, making it a practical solution for real-world word suggestion problems. Experimental evaluations confirm the model's effectiveness, revealing a substantial boost in prediction accuracy across various testing environments. The proposed model's success is, largely, a consequence of its ability to balance both semantic and syntactic word characteristics. A comprehensive simulation-based analysis highlighted the model's efficiency and feasibility. The proposed word suggestion model presents an attractive alternative to existing systems, offering a simple yet reliable solution. This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is addressed through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly eliminate disturbances, thus minimizing the time required for the swarm to reach its destination and ultimately lowering the energy consumption of this process. To quantify the extent of formation disturbance triggered by collision avoidance, deviation in the centroid of the swarm formation is measured, drawing inspiration from the concept of center of mass in classical mechanics. The study's experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed technique in terms of energy savings and completion time. Detailed analysis of the experiment reveals that the activation of the proposed formation maintenance strategy results in a 35.97% reduction in collision avoidance reformation time, also demonstrating linear scaling of the swarm size without energy consumption and completing the reformation process in significantly less time compared to conventional methods. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample is created to demonstrate the network's decisions, which is then used to train the compact model to replicate these decisions. This approach was successfully applied to various computer vision tasks with outstanding results, particularly for networks that were previously difficult to distill. Additionally, it was found that this method can also be effective in zero-shot settings for deriving compact models of existing networks. This study's findings could be valuable for researchers working with real-world applications where access to a network's parameters or training data may be limited. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training an conditional behavior model using only a cohort of untrained agents. We then develop a novel policy update rule that conditions the model on expert performance data, thereby augmenting the limited CoIL model with valuable, collective expertise. Experimental outcomes across multiple domains, including video games and fluid dynamics, reveal that CoIL supplements the model with a substantial amount of expertise, significantly outperforming conventional imitation learning and reinforcement learning. Furthermore, CoIL's performance surpasses state-of-the-art Cooperative Learning methods in complex, shared environment scenarios. Additionally, we provide theoretical insights into CoIL's expertise acquisition process. Our proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework represents a novel Cooperative Learning paradigm and serves as a versatile Co-Learning and expertise transfer method. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/fpjoseph/CoImitationLearning. The AIXEnvironment, a novel interactive environment with continuous, 2D fluid dynamics, is also available at https://github.com/fpjoseph/AIXEnvironment. We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange interaction that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Data from NMR, DC-susceptibility, and muon spin relaxation experiments support our theoretical findings and allow for an accurate extraction of the most relevant interlayer exchange interaction, which is around 0.05 times the in-plane coupling. Moreover, our research indicates that the XY anisotropy is field-tunable and can be adjusted by changing the hamiltonian's easy-axis direction. This distinctive property makes [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 a unique platform for investigating BKT physics in real materials. Additionally, we have established that this material remains in a quantum paramagnetic state down to 0.5 Kelvin, exhibiting a complex behavior near its critical coupling threshold. Using in-depth Monte Carlo simulations, we have identified the underlying origin of this threshold phenomenon, which is an intrinsic hallmark of materials that exhibit BKT transitions, and proposed a strategy to eliminate this issue and make [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 a true quantum paramagnet. Lastly, we have explored the link between the spin-correlation length and the near-neighbor mutual spin correlation in the XY plane as a ratio of these two quantities serves as a sensitive indicator of the BKT transition and potentially enables the estimation of the critical temperature. This study not only presents new findings but also significant modifications to the existing theoretical models for 2D and 3D BKT transitions that were previously considered unsolvable. Overall, this research enables the control of BKT correlations in magnetic materials through an external field, thereby opening up new avenues for field-induced changes in the spin correlation characteristics. Moreover, this study underscores the potential of [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 as a unique experimental testbed for the complex theoretical concepts underlying BKT transitions and provides valuable insights that can bridge the existing gap

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 26.4 days of observations and a data loss of 12%, resulting in an average of nearly 30 new spectroscopic measurements per night. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 15 nights for 3158 unique stellar targets and provided 18 new spectroscopic measurements per night. The analysis included measurements of stellar radial velocity, stellar parameters such as temperature and metallicity, and the analysis also helped in determining stellar mass and luminosity. A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice. With this approach, the Wilson coefficients can be accurately determined even when uncertainties are highly correlated. Additionally, this method allows for precise simultaneous extraction of the Wilson coefficients $C_9$ and $C_{9\'}$ and strongly reduces their sum by closely matching the $R_K$ anomaly's impact on these coefficients. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.  We evaluated several data augmentation techniques, including back-translation, transformer-generated paraphrases, and others, and found that a simple approach of rotating the sentence order produced the most consistent results across multiple topics.  Furthermore, our research revealed that a hybrid model combining a low-density graphical model and a transformer-based approach achieved an outstanding performance compared to competing methods.  We expect this finding to set a new benchmark for automated essay grading.  Additionally, our research identified key challenging phrases in the test set that were poorly predicted by the model, which could guide the design of more effective machine reading comprehension models.  The code and pre-trained models for this research are openly available on GitHub.  We intend for this research to be a significant contribution to the field of automated essay grading.  We hope that leveraging this knowledge, researchers can build upon and explore new approaches within this domain.  Our results are also expected to be helpful to practitioners in the educational sector who are seeking efficient and accurate automated essay grading solutions.  Finally, the models and code developed in this research can serve as a useful resource for the machine learning community, demonstrating the practical applications and research implications of advances in automated essay grading. Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples. Moreover, we provide a command-line tool to compute and visualize the geometry of marginal independence models along with their parameter spaces. This resource can be accessed at https://marginals.org/. At the same time, we introduce the R package Marginals, utilized in this work, that allows users to model, estimate, and analyze tensor decompositions and toric ideals associated with simplicial complexes and matroid independence sets. This package can be installed via R from https://mauzy.github.io/Marginals.html. In the future, we plan to enhance the package's capabilities by adding maximum likelihood estimation improvements and more efficiency optimizations. We envision the package will contribute to further research in marginal independence models. This work is a modified and extended version of the arXiv preprint 2001.04243. This research was partially supported by funding from the Alfred P. Sloan foundation's fellowship and the Data Science Institute's fellowship at the University of Chicago. We conducted our study in the Neubauer Laboratory for Data Science and the University of Chicago's Computation Institute. We conducted an exploratory analysis in R and Python to initiate this research, and we used Stan for parameter estimation. We are grateful to Michael Kirkup and Alasdair Bremner for their collaboration and expertise, particularly on matroid independence models, and to Andrew Tauscher for his early work on marginal independence models. We appreciate Benjamin Draski's feedback on our research and Raman Arunathan's help with installing the Marginals package. Finally, we thank Josh Chen and the UChicago student group BAYES for their inquiries and feedback on our research and package. Stan and R are now used in a new command-line tool, StanR, that we introduced to make it easier for users to model tensor decompositions and toric ideals associated with simplicial complexes and matroids through marginal independence models. This tool can be installed via https://mauzy.github.io/StANR.html. We conducted our research in the Neubauer Laboratory for Data Science and the University of Chicago

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings in a more realistic framework. Furthermore, our model provides a foundation for investigating how different social mobility patterns impact opportunity distribution. Lastly, our model enables examination of the impact of various social mobility modifications in a controlled environment. The study is relevant to the allocation of opportunities, such as college admissions, lottery tickets, and family planning slots, among others. The findings can also be applied to the context of primary care visits, which can be seen as opportunities that are limited and allocated on a priority basis. The study is particularly tailored to examine primary care visits in a controlled setting, although its implications can be extended to other contexts. The analysis offers a framework that can be used to investigate how various social mobility patterns impact, and are affected by, the allocation of opportunities. The study offers a model-based approach that can help understand and mitigate the effects of social mobility on opportunity distribution, which can provide insights that are sensitive to data and are equally relevant in controlled and natural settings. The result can be applied to situations such as college admissions, where, depending on the social mobility scenario, it can be beneficial or not to prioritize students from lower socioeconomical backgrounds. Similarly, in a scenario where socioeconomical status does not affect mobility, it can be beneficial to prioritize students from lower socioeconomical backgrounds. The result can also be applied to primary care, where prioritizing patients based on socioeconomical status may not always be beneficial. The analysis offers a general model that can help understand the effects of social mobility on opportunity distribution and provide insights that can be useful in controlled and natural settings. The result can be applied to various social mobility scenarios and can provide a framework for investigating, and potentially mitigating, the effects of social mobility on opportunity distribution. The study offers a model-based approach that can help understand the relationship between social mobility and opportunity distribution,

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also demonstrate that degree-degree correlations can be efficiently addressed using the Gaussian approximation, and showcase the accuracy of our error analysis through both theoretical and numerical justifications. We anticipate that the development of LDPC designs incorporating degree-degree correlations will yield superior error rates and greater design flexibility. Furthermore, our work may be extended to various other error-correcting code ensembles. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive safety filter design for a hard real-time operating system on microcontrollers, which is subsequently used to demonstrate safety on a quadcopter. The associated software and hardware can be accessed via a publicly available repository. This research was supported by ANR project reference ANR-17-CE22-039- and ARC2 challenge funding. The related dataset can be accessed at: https://doi.org/10.6087189.1591.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states. Furthermore, this knowledge can be applied to other quantum communication protocols to undermine their security. If successfully implemented, this attack could compromise the security of numerous QKD networks and eavesdrop on related communications. However, our novel attack requires the source phase to be randomly altered, a condition that is naturally prevented by using binary QKD systems such as quantum key distribution using weak coherent states and fast-phase randomization. Our work presents a new approach to quantum key distribution, highlighting that fast-phase randomization in binary systems makes them significantly more resilient to hacking compared to phase-encoding systems. As such, this research has significant practical implications and can improve the security of QKD networks employing binary key distribution. To test our attack in a real-world setting, we developed a practical quantum hacking tool. Due to space constraints, the details of the tool will be disclosed in a separate article. Our research offers an important contribution by demonstrating the susceptibility of source phase randomness to attack, thereby undermining the security of QKD systems, and by prototyping this attack using a 2x2 quantum key distribution test platform. This has enabled us to develop and execute a practical quantum hacking tool, thereby illustrating the vulnerability of existing QKD systems through a real-world example. In addition, our research presents an innovative approach to hacking QKD systems by utilizing hybrid measurements that are both quantum and classical in nature, utilizing only basic optical and electronic components, and highlighting the limitations of current quantum key distribution protocols that rely on randomizing the source phase to a limited degree, thereby compromising its security. Finally, our research has delivered a practical quantum hacking tool, thereby illustrating the vulnerability of existing QKD systems through a real-world example. This research has significant practical implications by illustrating the vulnerability of existing QKD systems through a real-world example, and presenting an innovative approach to quantum key distribution

For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive experiment using a 1.5 billion parameter model, investigating the effect of different training datasets on the few-shot learning capacity. Our findings indicate that models trained on diverse datasets, such as Wikipedia, exhibit improved out-of-distribution performance when performing few-shot tasks compared to those trained on broader datasets like Wikipedia plus English articles. Moreover, our research reveals that the model's performance in few-shot learning is directly correlated with the distractor data's semantic relatedness to the target task, and that using a large dataset like Wikipedia alone cannot convey this semantic relatedness to the model. Our study's results also suggest that models trained on diverse datasets are more susceptible to overfitting when encountering in-context training data. To address this, we propose a simple strategy to mitigate overfitting when performing few-shot learning with large language models. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Our research extends the understanding of large language models' few-shot learning capabilities and identifies potential areas of optimization. It also opens up potential avenues for tailored dataset selection to enhance the models' in-context learning capacity. Moreover, our study's findings have implications for data labeling and resource allocation, suggesting that working with smaller datasets with high semantic relatedness may be more beneficial than using a large dataset with low relatedness. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that Wikipedia alone is an excellent training corpus for large language models performing few-shot learning, and that further research may be needed to find an even more optimal training corpus. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens to the remaining gas after it leaves the cooling radius. To investigate this, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations with varying parameters, including thermal conduction, magnetic fields, and radiative cooling. Our model predicts the thermal conduction rate to be around 10 to the power of 3 to the power of 8, which is roughly the same as the collisional ionization equilibrium conductivity in similar systems. Ultimately, we found that the cooling process leads to the development of a near-equilibrium state between thermal conduction and radiative cooling in the innermost regions of the gas cloud. A steady-state is achieved by balancing conduction and cooling rates, causing the gas cloud to shrink at a predictable rate. Our model also indicates magnetic fields with strengths of around 5 to the power of minus 1 Gauss have a conducting opacity similar to that of other systems. A sudden increase in the magnetic field's strength causes the gas cloud to grow as the balance between thermal conduction and radiative cooling reverses, resulting in a prolonged, unstable growth. Additionally, we observed that a steeply rising external magnetic field causes the gas cloud to grow even more. Conversely, a flatly rising external magnetic field has little effect on the gas cloud's stability or its tendency to grow. Overall, we found that the gas cloud's stability is heavily dependent on the balance between thermal conduction and radiative cooling, while its growth is largely determined by the external magnetic field's slope. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is the increased growth driven by the dynamo process. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside an iterative geometric refinement process. Evaluation on various datasets reveals PRNet's ability to consistently find corresponding points and achieve superior results across multiple metrics without the need for ground truth. Moreover, PRNet maintains fast run times, with <1 minute for aligning 10240 points, demonstrating the framework's efficiency and versatility. As a versatile framework, PRNet can be applied to a wide range of tasks including object registration, shape retrieval, and 3D pose estimation. The code will be made available for these tasks. As a leading method in this space, PRNet is expected to spur development in areas like robotic manipulation, industrial assembly, and medical imaging, where partial point cloud registration plays a critical role. The influence of PRNet is further exemplified by its applications in object manipulation, shape retrieval, 3D pose estimation, and medical image registration, among others. Moreover, PRNet's performance can be leveraged for tasks not confined to partial point clouds, demonstrating its versatility. The novel concepts underpinning PRNet are:  (1) employing a keypoint detector for intermediate supervision; (2) using iterative geometric refinement for performance enhancement; (3) leveraging the suitability of suitable representations for complex geometric data; (4) performing self-supervised learning for intermediate supervision, serving as a stopping criterion, and facilitating generalization across seen and unseen shapes. The particular training data used to develop the keypoint detector are model-based, comprising 80% easy cases and 20% harder ones. Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with other computational models including non-local thermal equilibrium spectral line calculations and a radiative transfer model that incorporates dust formation, which predicts a distinct near-ultraviolet continuum peak. This is followed by a comparative examination of the predicted continuum spectra with observational data including IUE, HST, and FOS spectra of the AD Leo flare. Lastly, a plot of the model parameters that best fit the near-ultraviolet continuum data is presented, along with estimates of the radiative flux of the electron beam model. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for each category. Additionally, we design a specific validation protocol tailored to frequency patterns observed in numerous real-world datasets. Experimental results on various frequency patterns and point cloud datasets, including SunCG, SCAPES, and SemanticKITTI, demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC, not only achieving significant enhancements in validation efficiency but also verifying the frequency-based optimization of general robustness validation strategies, thereby providing up to two times faster validation compared to the current best approach. All validation strategies and frequency analysis data are available on our GitHub repository for others to use. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation methods' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. 
The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/juliusbennets/Time\_LowFER. 
Our benchmark is also available at https://github.com/juliusbennets/TGLFER.

However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a synthetic network, the non-integer dimensional analysis of the Lorenz system, and the analysis of chaotic galaxy collisions. Furthermore, the approach is applied to the European Power System to identify clusters of consumption patterns. The analysis reveals that the power grid can be divided into distinct geographical groups characterized by distinct time-series patterns. These findings provide insights into the underlying structure of the power grid and may be used to inform the design of smart energy systems. The proposed method is positioned as a pioneering approach to cluster analysis that can serve as a versatile tool for detecting communities in dynamic systems. The associated algorithms and data are available for download on the provided website. This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered. We demonstrate that, despite initial appearances, the proposed methods are not significantly more complicated than traditional techniques. In particular, we show that combining them does not exponentially increase processing time. We also provide conditions under which monitoring is possible without relying on expensive model checking techniques and identify limitations for certain property types. This revisited monitoring approach offers simplified online algorithms and clearer understanding of monitoring's computational complexity. As such, it paves the way for more practical real-time monitoring implementations. Moreover, this work offers insights into the precise computational complexity of deciding whether a run satisfies a given property, including cases where it is possible with linear effort and others that require exponential effort. We rectify apparent shortcomings in earlier studies on this topic and offer a comprehensive picture of the complexity of deciding property satisfaction, including the effects of model simplification and the advantages of exploiting run-specific information. Ultimately, this paper identifies the inherent complexity limitations of monitoring real-time systems. In particular, we show that, in certain situations, exponential online complexity is unavoidable. Nevertheless, we also offer a parameterized algorithm that efficiently decides the satisfaction of properties under specific conditions, thus addressing an earlier suggestion by Alur and Henzinger. We also offer an online algorithm that provides a heuristic solution to this problem that is additive logarithmic in the underlying time units. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center issue - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] hardness class, whereas we find it relatively simpler with doubling dimension values. This distinction is the first documented case where a problem exhibits W[1] hardness with highway dimension, despite being manageable with doubling dimension values. To achieve these results, we derive new scheme formulations, offering an alternative to the traditional starting tree approach, by utilizing doubling dimension based bipartite graph representations and establishing the highway dimension equivalent '6-hop' graph representation, which may be of independent interest. Our findings are also extended to the more general $k$-Supplier issue, yielding similar parameterized solution schemes. All our proposed schemes incorporate efficient dynamic programming and branching strategies to achieve optimal results. This research is expected to contribute to the expanding field of dimension-based complexity classification in algorithm design and, by extension, to the expanding area of algorithmic fractal complexity classification. Additionally, our study may find applications in routing and network design scenarios where doubling and highway dimension properties apply. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority. For example, on HMDB-51, HAN surpasses state-of-the-art
models by 2.7% and 3.6% in terms of accuracy when trained on NTU105-Skeleton and
NTU105-Video datasets, respectively. The proposed model is open-source and can be
accessed at the link provided at the end of this abstract. The code can be found at: https://github.com/SagivLP/HAN. The model's demonstrations are available at: https://sagivlp.github.io/HAN. \\

The final model's 1,024-dimensional features are generated by a $1 \times 1$ convolution
that follows the last fusion mechanism within the primary network, as described in the
stipulated schedule. The class which the feature belongs to is then determined by a
softmax function applied to a weighted version of this feature. The weighted feature
itself is produced by multiplying the original feature by the attention weight associated
with its respective class, which is calculated using a separate $1 \times 1$ convolution
applied to the feature. The same approach applies to the secondary network, whose output is
then combined with that of the primary network via a softmax function to produce the
final attention weight for each class. The combined outputs of both networks are then
inputted into a $1 \times 1$ convolution that generates the final set of hierarchical
attention weights. The mechanism by which this model captures the hierarchy of actions
within complex videos is then combined with two-dimensional graph embedding and fast
residual network to produce the model's outstanding performance in action recognition.\\

The proposed model, Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), is evaluated on three action

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe. We will introduce the concept of "protostar darkness" – a stage of SF characterized by a decrease in radiation intensity – and explore how it occurs. We will also discuss the protostar protoplanetary disk system, focusing on how it is formed, and highlighting its similarity to the solar system. We will examine whether the conditions of a particular star formation resemble those of our solar system, and explore the implications of this examination, particularly concerning the universe's potential to support life. We will conclude by discussing recent findings from the James Webb Space Telescope, highlighting its capabilities and looking forward to future observations. We hypothesize that "protostar darkness" occurs due to the absorption of radiation by charged particles and dust, marking the beginning of a distinct phase of star formation. This stage is, we propose, universally present in star formation, and is followed by a period of illumination as the protostar's energy releases. During this illumination, the protostar grows more massive, and its energy drives the formation of a circumstellar disk. This 'dark' and then 'bright' period may be indicative of a binary or multiple star system formation. Observing this process in other star systems is made possible by the rapid advancements in space technology and ground-breaking research, and paves the way for future advancements, particularly in the James Webb Space Telescope, and future projects such as the Giant Antennas for Millimeter-Wave Universe Observation, and the Extremely Large Telescope. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or data. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or provide real-time predictions during real-time operations. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing computing and data storage requirements for feature extraction. By comparing its accuracy with existing high-performance classifiers, NBcoded demonstrates a comparable 97% attack detection rate with a significantly reduced error rate of 1%. The subsequent benchmarking tests on low-resource devices, such as the Raspberry Pi, showcase NBcoded's ability to operate efficiently even on hardware with limited processing power, achieving a remarkable 45fps on the Raspberry Pi 4. Moreover, a freely downloadable NBcoded virtual appliance is available on multiple cloud platforms for community use. NBcoded's training data is also shared on GitHub to support the development of future research in network attack classification. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, is examined, showing that it has no general method for finding an optimal solution, as evidenced by the fact that finding an overall best match may require computationally expensive processes. However, we present a polynomial-time algorithm for finding stable matchings in scenarios with one-dimensional valuations and provide an alternative, slower approach applicable to any valuation type. Furthermore, we present some criteria under which we can guarantee the existence of the optimal solution in certain cases. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Our results indicate that, in comparison to best-known classic decoding algorithms, the reinforcement learning decoders achieve a 11% improvement in circuit failure rate and a 34% improvement in circuit latency within a failure rate threshold. To facilitate wider adoption, the underlying framework and tools have been made accessible through an open-source release attached to this article. This includes the SourceHut codebase and a pre-built Docker image that allow for seamless replication of our results. This research further offers a versatile quantum decoding platform that can be used to investigate many other environments and applications. Moreover, the approach outlined has broader implications for other problem domains where classical decoding challenges apply, and it might be adapted to solve diverse machine learning problems. Finally, in a related development, our finding that reinforcement learning can be effectively applied to decode quantum errors has sparked discussions on its potential limitations, and our responses to those concerns are also included in this article. This research contributes to ongoing efforts to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing in various fields. To ensure the results can be reproduced, the source code used in this article is made available at https://sourcehut.org/organizations/posipit/-/repositories/1449/ and a Docker image is available at docker.io/posipit/qldec is also included in the article. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality. This method also serves as a suitable vehicle for educational purposes in demonstrating the capabilities of quantum physics in real-world applications. This research is presented in the form of a published letter in Physical Review A. 

Keywords: quantum metrology, quantum feedback control, entanglement, interferometry, quantum physics, quantum information, laser optics, optical systems, quantum mechanics, quantum physics experiments.

The presence of two variables in meta-regression analyses also necessitates techniques that can effectively handle non-positive definite estimated variance-covariance matrices that may arise due to small sample sizes or the presence of outliers and heterogeneous study data. The proposed estimators address these issues by incorporating cluster-specific variance components into their models and providing an alternative to the standard pooled estimator when data points are correlated. The application of these estimators is demonstrated through the analysis of a dataset consisting of 22 clinical trials in meta-regression based on secondary endpoints with associated covariates. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems with non-volatile memory. This method involves introducing algorithmic checkpoints that incorporate both explicit flushes of the system cache into main memory and verification of data integrity. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the ergodicity of initial configurations, the distribution of lifetimes, and the probability density of final energies for individual bodies. Our results showed that the flux-based statistical model accurately predicts all measured quantities, surpassing previous predictions based on binary interactions. Furthermore, the flux-based model exhibits exceptional agreement across various measures, exhibiting statistical uncertainties that are typically only associated with statistical errors of approximately 0.5%, which is consistent with our previous theoretical expectation. This level of statistical precision is directly attributable to the high number of ergodic disintegrations that occur in non-hierarchical three-body systems. Moreover, our findings reveal that the flux-based statistical model is equally effective for systems with equal masses and those with mass ratios, thus validating the statistical approach. These limits may be particularly useful in analyzing and interpreting the data from exoplanet and star cluster environments using statistical three-body models. Lastly, our investigation led to the realization that the ergodic distribution of final energies is independent of any underlying symmetries in the system, which has significant implications for the inverse problem of three-body dynamics. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Our framework is versatile, allowing it to be applied to related calculi such as the probabilistic lambda calculus with angles (PCLÁ) and the probabilistic lambda calculus with tests (PLCT). As a concrete example, we develop a denotational semantics for the stochastic lambda calculus and use it to prove operational and denotational equivalences for a meta-morphic transformation on a probabilistic circuit proposed in another study (Guerrini et al., 2019). This demonstrates that our semantics is practical and can be used for refining and verifying probabilistic algorithms. All technical proofs in this research have been formalized and made available in a Coq mode available for download. This research contributes to the goal of enabling formal reasoning about the high-level functional programming of probabilistic algorithms before and after transformation. By extending this research to leverage recent improvements in the categorical semantics of the stochastic lambda calculus (Guerrini et al., 2020), this research may also enable the composition of deterministic and probabilistic refinements in a unified framework. This could ultimately facilitate the integration of high-level probabilistic programming languages with efficient and native support for quantum and probabilistic circuits. As a result, this research may ultimately contribute to the development of hybrid programs that combine quantum and probabilistic methods, with a focus on high-level functional programming techniques. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets. They can utilize this tool to mine designs from their organization's discussion data and tailor these models to suit their specific requirements. In addition to these resources, we have published a detailed guide on design mining, encompassing theoretical foundations, model implementations, and usage examples, which can be accessed via the Software Engineering Research Institute guide. This research is part of a larger effort to apply machine learning techniques to software engineering, as evident in the ongoing work on code review mining. We believe our approach to design mining can be extended to other topics within software engineering and are exploring its potential applications. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate effective discussion classification, enhancing developers' ability to manage and utilize their team discussions, meetings, and online comments. We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A major uncertainty in the early universe arises from the origin of the heavily amplified magnetic fields that form around the first massive stars. Recent numerical studies have investigated the magnetic field's role in disrupting the disks of these Population III stars but yielded conflicting results. To resolve this discrepancy, we have examined how the amplification of magnetic fields affects the disks of these stars in a series of high-resolution simulations. By focusing on the physical processes that determine the initial structure of the protostellar disk, we identified the critical factors driving disk fragmentation. Our results indicate that an exponentially amplified magnetic field with a 10-gauss strength at a few thousand kilometers can prevent the fragmentation of the protostellar disk. However, a constant magnetic field of similar strength has a negligible effect on the disk's fragmentation. We have found that the key to these findings lies in the dynamic balance between the disk's inner and outer regions, caused by the protostar's gravitational pull and the electric current generated by the disk's rotation. This balance, combined with the radial influx of angular momentum, prevents the inner disk from collapsing and generates unstable layers that drive convective motions. Due to the disk's instability and the dynamic balance between the disk's inner and outer regions, the dynamically unstable objects cannot survive the violent convective motions that affect the protostellar disk. Conversely, in the case of a constant magnetic field, the protostellar disk's structure differs significantly from the exponentially amplified field scenario, resulting in a disk that is unstable and fragmented. However, a change in the protostar's mass affects the dynamic balance between the disk's inner and outer regions, caused by its gravitational pull and the electric current generated by the disk's rotation. This finding indicates that the nature of the amplified magnetic field is unique and cannot be replaced by a constant magnetic field strength. Additionally, we have discovered that the metallicity of the collapsing cloud has a minimal effect on the protostellar disk's structure but can alter the nature of the amplified magnetic field. This is a novel finding, as it suggests that the exponentially amplified magnetic field is not solely the result of primordial gas but may also be influenced by metals present in the collapsing cloud. In the course of these simulations, we have identified several unique features of the protostellar disk's structure that are consistent across various magnetic field scenarios. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within three and five years by 17 percent and 15 percent, respectively.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in recidivism leads to net gains of $1.13 and $3.02 per dollar spent on mental health treatment in the first three and five years, respectively.  The data also reveals that 41 percent of initially eligible offenders did not receive the required mental health treatment, leading to the suggestion that better follow-up with offenders and ways to decrease initial noncompliance are potential areas for further improvement.  Overall, this research highlights the positive effect of court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation on recidivism and indicates providing this treatment to convicted individuals could lead to significant criminal justice system cost savings.  The research has potential to decrease crime and expenses in the justice system through the provision of court-ordered mental health treatment.  Future studies could build upon this research by analyzing data that extends beyond North Carolina, making the results more generalizable, and could also examine various factors that influence whether convicted individuals comply with the treatment.  Furthermore, it is also suggested that follow-up with offenders could be improved by developing new sentencing options that blend mental health treatment with incarceration in a controlled setting, such as a halfway house. Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been developed to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time. This capability has been further utilized to estimate the initial map uncertainty before data collection begins. A mathematical proof has established that the proposed algorithm is unbiased and that the expected map error decreases at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of data points collected. Experiments have demonstrated that the map error can be reduced by the factor already mentioned and that the proposed approach requires significantly fewer measurements than traditional methods to achieve the same accuracy. Additionally, a method has been developed to assess the reliability of the estimated map and the potential locations where the map may need to be updated to achieve better results in other applications. The proposed approach has been evaluated in extensive simulations and field experiments using a customized drone equipped with a U-bloxx GPS sensor, a magnetometer, a barometer, a temperature and humidity sensor, and a radio frequency signal strength sensor. The reliability of the designed sensor platform was verified through the analysis of the experimental data. The experimental site, an outdoor parking lot, featured terrain features that fell outside the expected parameters used to optimize the map, causing the system to successfully adapt to the actual environment through a series of tests. The proposed approach has also been compared to other UAV-based radio map estimation techniques using benchmark performance metrics. All the source code and experimental data are available for reproduction of the results. The future research directions, potential applications, and potential impacts have also been outlined. The likelihood of observing a time window with $k$ ones (anomaly occurrences) in a $d$-dimensional gauge sequence of length $N$ is calculated as the probability of two binary states transitioning into $N$ and the probability of $k$ ones occurring among $N$ dimensions. A high likelihood indicates the presence of anomalies in the gauge data. In our analysis, anomaly detection is demonstrated using gauge data from simulated cosmic strings. The approach can be adapted to accommodate various Markov model-based statistical models. Furthermore, this technique's adaptability extends to various fields beyond cosmic string analysis. Its versatility makes it an invaluable tool for identifying anomalies in signal data. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared error loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. Additionally, this work discusses how estimating a mixture component's mean by selecting a single mixture component and averaging its parameters is equivalent to solving the problem through GMLE's framework. Several extensions to the GMLE's theory are proposed, including 1) accounting for model misspecification, 2) relaxing the standard assumption that the parameters $\theta_i$ are distinct, and 3) estimating a mixture component's mean while also accounting for a parameter other than mean variation. These generalizations provide valuable insights and show the versatility of the GMLE's framework. Furthermore, this note provides estimates of $\eta_G$ for data sets that have been previously analyzed, including data sets related to programming, evolution, and genetics.
