OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy. Finally, the research evaluates the effectiveness of the proposed technique using real data sets. Results indicate that the proposed mechanism can yield better utility while maintaining the same level of privacy as compared to existing approaches. Moreover, the study reveals that the amount of privacy breach due to inter-record dependence can be substantial. Hence, the proposed mechanism is valuable in practical data analysis applications that involve dependencies between data records. We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated. The regularity of these paths results in the regularity of the measure, allowing the regularity of the Lagrangian to be lifted and thus enabling the determination of an equilibrium in this context. The regularity of these paths also enables the application of standard PDE techniques to solve the collaborative system of equations that define the mean field game, yielding a solution with a regular transition profile. The transition profile is regular due to the application of the maximum principle and the smoothness of the solution to the backward stochastic PDE that defines the mean field game, a regular transition profile in turn defines the measure that represents the joint state and control distribution. The solution to the mean field game is thus shown to exist under these constrained conditions. The regularity of these paths can also be applied to study the continuous dependence of the mean field game solution on the Lagrangian function, yielding the dependence only in relation to the norm of the Lagrangian function rather than its Lipschitz constant. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures, we determined they do not exhibit the characteristic spread around their center expected from structures traveling together through space. Instead, their members appear connected through dotting patterns, likely resulting from Gaia's resolution limits and random scatter in measurement data, hence their members are not actually part of these structures. Furthermore, these structures' members exhibit varying ages and chemical properties, contradicting the notion they share a common origin. We conclude that these structures are mere illusions, a result of Gaia's measurement errors, and their members actually comprise loosely associated stars that have always been loosely grouped in space. We suggest re-classifying these structures as "stellar clusters" with ages and sizes that can be determined through further analysis. By doing so, we ensure that these structures are not incorrectly attributed to theories of star formation or astrophysical simulation models before their validity has been verified. Ultimately, this study serves as a reminder that even the most advanced data can hide biases and limitations that must be factored in when conducting scientific analysis. We propose that these structures, now referred to as "stellar clusters", be studied as part of the Gaia Data Release 3, where we can employ more robust and reliable analysis tools to gain new insights into their nature. We envision a future publication demonstrating that these "stellar clusters" exhibit ages ranging from 200 million to 2.5 billion years and diameters from 5 to 80 light-years. We anticipate that these results will be consistent with the simulated outcomes of astrophysical formation models. We have pre-registered these expectations as of 2022-08-25. We are now conducting further analysis to confirm these predictions and are preparing to share the results at an upcoming scientific meeting where we will present our findings in detail. The results of this project, including its results and methodology, can be found on a public scientific platform. We have also shared the code and data used in this research on a public scientific repository. We plan to make the rest of the results available soon. The Gaia data we studied are publicly available, and we employed publicly available and custom-coded software to conduct our analysis. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We've based our analysis on how the scalar potentials in four and five-dimensional theories are linked. Our findings indicate that in five-dimensional theories with a stable vacuum, a micron-scale extra dimension is likely standard issue for all supersymmetric theories. We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region. Additionally, we identify specific conditions under which the transformed patches will be geodesically complete. For singular values of the Hopf differential, we discover new singular solutions to the Codazzi equation. Moreover, we apply the Darboux transformation to a specific net on the figure-eight surface to generate a family of compact rotationally symmetric surfaces. Finally, we use the Calapso transformation to generate a family of non-compact rotationally symmetric surfaces. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in the task of link prediction. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention. This paper proposes a novel approach called TME-UA, a unified architecture that integrates the benefits of two distinct methods, the multiple and the unitary, offering both the ability to model transitions across time and a compact representation of temporal relationships. We experimentally evaluate TME-UA by comparing it to established models such as TME, UA, TKE, TGCN, and KBC. Data from Wikidata and KnowledgeGraphBenchmark was used for the evaluation, which revealed that the proposed method outperforms the existing models across various settings. This improvement is attributed to the ability of TME-UA to model temporal relationships and transitions, as well as its ability to capture the general properties of entities and their relationships through the unitary component. Furthermore, we investigate the ethical implications of our method by analyzing its performance on groups of entities that share certain characteristics. This study provides insights into how temporal embeddings impact our understanding of entities that are associated with temporal data. We present a method called KEA that analyzes distributional attributes of entities to identify patterns and groups of entities. Then, within these groups, we evaluate the performance of TME-UA and find that for certain groups, notable improvements in link prediction performance occur when using the proposed method. This research offers several contributions: (i) the development of a novel, technically strong method called TME-UA that outperforms existing models; (ii) the investigation of how temporal KGE models impact our understanding of the properties of the entities, as revealed by their distribution of temporal attributes, (iii) the identification of entity groups that benefit from the use of the proposed method, and (iv) the provide of code and data to replicate the results for other researchers. This work follows the guidelines for Machine Learning and Knowledge Graphs, leading to new knowledge through the analysis of these techniques. The code for this research is publicly available at https://github.com/josealvarez/TME-UA. Wakim, et al. To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices. Also, our method naturally provides support for following multiple instructions and answering multi-step questions. You can try it out on our new question-answering dataset, called K-QA, which contains over 100,000 questions that require knowledge graph reasoning. K-QA is based on real wedding planning scenarios and is available for free. We've also made OREO-LM's code and knowledge graph reasoner open-source so everyone can use them. Experimental results show that OREO-LM significantly outperforms other language models on K-QA by 8.5% and also works well with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, to greatly improve their performance. We observed similar gains in performance on other question-answering tasks, including SQuAD and CoQA. Also, our method doesn't need any special annotations in the data to train, which makes it even more useful. We're excited about the potential of this technology and how it can be used to answer questions in daily life, such as which wedding venue is closest to my office? or what are the top ratings for this product?, and we hope it will inspire more research in this area. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The extraordinary HII region in UGC 8839 could indicate a distant dwarf galaxy is influencing its outer disk. The finding also raises questions about the potential impact of a similar interaction on the formation and development of dark matter in galaxies. The research further highlights the significance of more in-depth, high-resolution studies required to comprehend various dynamical elements influencing galaxy evolution. The analysis includes novel findings on galaxy morphology, and offers a fresh perspective on the persistent, enigmatic Malin 1 system. The data collection and analysis for this research were primarily based on archival SDSS, 2MASS, and other publicly available datasets. The study identifies several unexplored aspects of galaxy interaction, and suggests further observation of UGC 8839 and Malin 1 to shed more light on the unusual dynamics in both galaxies. The research also proposes an extensive, high-resolution study of 56 spiral galaxies, and suggests three potential candidates - NGC 4136, UGC 8839, and U12410+7222 - which exhibit certain characteristics similar to UGC 8839 and warrant further examination. The analysis includes new data on these galaxies, and highlights their shared dynamical features. The research also includes a general study on the dynamics of 16 fragile, faint spiral galaxies, and reveals their shared characteristic of minimal star formation except in their outer rims. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. The findings also result in the first-ever extraction of the photon-proton coupling constant at the 5% level of precision, alongside the derivation of the photon-photon luminosity, serving as a crucial reference for the investigation of saturation phenomena in the rapidity distribution. The subsequent sections delve into the implications of these findings for the investigation of the photon-photon coupling

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through its computation of the Shapley value for a dataset containing over 66,000 examples and a query involving over 10,000 features. The system's functionality is centered on a novel data streaming model, referred to as Shapley streams, designed to facilitate the computation of the Shapley value for training examples in an end-to-end machine learning pipeline through an iterative process. The system's functionality also includes an algorithm for annotating training examples based on their computed Shapley value, referred to as Shapley annotate. A comprehensive experimental evaluation of DataScope has been conducted to assess its performance, using a combination of real and synthetic datasets, by evaluating its two key components: the correctness of its theoretical foundations and the scalability of its implementation. The evaluation revealed that DataScope is capable of accurately computing the Shapley value for an unprecedented level of data diversity, and its algorithm is designed to be both efficient and adaptable to a range of machine learning pipelines. Furthermore, DataScope's implementation demonstrates a several-orders-of-magnitude improvement in running time compared to state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods, and its functionality is both easy to understand and use. This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices. Focusing on even-dimensional scenarios, we examine orthogonal and Lorentzian structures on posets of positive definite or positive semi-definite matrices. These structures have implications for the topological properties of the matrix poset itself, as well as the algebraic properties of the ideals associated with it. Furthermore, we investigate the enumerative geometry of the resulting posets, revealing connections to the breaking parameter space of the matrix poset and the tropical nullcone. The relationships we establish also provide new perspectives on existing results, such as Barany's theorem and the Combinatorial Theorems of Cox, Eisenbud, and Schenck. Additionally, we identify key questions and areas for further research. The content of this text significantly builds upon the author's 2014 PhD dissertation. The underlying ideas have been developed over many years of the author's training at the University of Minnesota. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction analysis indicates that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that when Mn$_3$Sn enters the helical state, its in-plane lattice parameter exhibits unusual temperature dependence, supporting the hypothesis that atom rearrangement is necessary for the material's new magnetic property. The findings underscore the significance of controlling pressure in manipulating Mn$_3$Sn's magnetic ground states and associated anomalous Hall effect. The research also forecasts potential opportunities for pressure-controlled switching of the anomalous Hall effect in similar materials featuring the same $A$$_{3}$Mn$_{3}$X composition. The study also proposes that Mn$_3$Ge, another material with a similar structure, may also exhibit pressure-dependent changes in its magnetic ground states. The research discovers that when subjected to pressure, Mn$_3$Ge undergoes a transformation from a helical state to a completely collapsed state that eliminates the anomalous Hall effect. The investigation provides substantial evidence that controlled pressure can be utilized to induce new modes of anomalous Hall effect in robust, stable, and practical antiferromagnetic materials. The study paves the way for further research on the material properties of Mn$_3$Sn and similar compounds by applying pressure. The research also forecasts the potential for these materials to be utilized in the development of reliable spin-based electronics and other cutting-edge devices. The study further provides new perspectives for controlling the material properties of triangular antiferromagnets through pressure, while also offering significant insights into the material's magnetic ground states, the processes that drive them, and the resulting material properties. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Our analysis also provides a detailed understanding of the smoothness of the first eigenfunction. Furthermore, we find that the first eigenvalue exhibits a dramatic change when the parameter $\beta$ transitions from a positive value to a negative value, and we also investigate the asymptotic behavior of the first eigenvalue as the parameter $r$ increases or decreases without bound. Our analysis further reveals that the first eigenvalue attains its minimum value at $\beta = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\sigma_1(\partial \Omega_0)}{|\Omega_0|}$, where $\sigma_1(\partial \Omega_0)$ is the first Steklov eigenvalue of the boundary operator on $\partial \Omega_0$, and $|\Omega_0|$ is the Lebesgue measure of the set $\Omega_0$. Additionally, we make a conjecture about the second eigenvalue and provide supporting reasoning. Our findings also imply that the first Robin eigenvalue undergoes a similar transition when the parameter $\beta$ changes sign. Our analysis makes use of suitable trial functions that combine aspects of the first Steklov eigenfunction of the given problem and a radial function that decays or increases without bound. Our study is closely related to the works of Herrmann and Vessella and Herrmann and Rosier. Our analysis does not rely on specific technical assumptions that were employed in those studies, and we therefore provide an alternative approach to their results. Our study also makes use of Poincaré-Friedrichs inequality as well as hardy-type inequalities. Our analysis provides new insights and perspectives on the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions. Our study examines the smoothness of the eigenfunctions, and we make a conjecture about the second eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions. Our analysis implies the existence of a first eigenvalue for the first Steklov-Robin problem and provides a first eigenvalue for the first Steklov problem.

To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. Lastly, we successfully apply this method to examine the influence of carrier-induced spatial radiation on directional emission in microcavity lasers. This approach offers a versatile tool for evaluating directional emission in various optical systems. Additionally, this study discloses its potential to the best of our knowledge for the first time. Please refer to the following article for more information: Chen et al, Light: Science & Applications, 2021, 10.1002/lspa.244. Abstract only.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby indicating accurate predictions. The outcomes of this study unambiguously demonstrate the existence of a stable relationship between cryptocurrency prices and their comparators' daily returns. This evidence can be attributed to the theory of induced information, which proposes that the investment decisions of speculators are not randomly distributed and are instead connected to the future value of the underlying asset, thereby inducing relationships among daily returns. Unlike prior studies, which have attempted to model price movements using techniques such as ARIMA, our approach focuses on detecting patterns within returns and analyzing their relationships over time. By doing so, we believe we have made a significant contribution to the field of cryptocurrency research. Additionally, our findings have practical implications for investors, who can rely on the stability of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, a medium of exchange, to make informed investment decisions. The code used for this study's analysis is available on GitHub at https://github.com/galtsco/cryptostability. Futures works will focus on extending the induced information approach to incorporate fundamental variables and investigate the role of speculation in driving relationships among daily returns. Moreover, we aim to broaden the scope of our analysis to include other assets, such as commodity prices and stock indexes, as well as explore the connections between relationships among returns and the underlying business cycles. By pushing the induced information approach to its theoretical limits, we are confident that we can develop a comprehensive understanding of the concepts of money and medium of exchange. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we discover its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions. The precise large deviation results we obtain can also be applied to other related scenarios such as quasi-constant initial conditions and the impact of a step function change in the drift term on KPZ dynamics. Our work also enables a novel re-interpretation of the weak noise theory as a universal, integrable component of KPZ dynamics. Furthermore, the large deviation results we obtain can be applied to other probabilistic problems including the dynamics of a particle in a disordered, diffusive medium and a model of group dynamics that exhibits a 'gang effect.' Finally, we speculate that the solutions presented here may also apply to other stochastic partial differential equations such as the dynamics of a nonlinear beam. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications. This modified approach is also expected to be applicable to fourth-generation hard X-ray linear and recirculating electron linear accelerators, enabling the delivery of high-intensity pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds. Furthermore, this modification can be implemented in various tapering schemes, such as sawtooth and tinook modules, to optimize performance. This work was facilitated by the SARAYA cluster computing resource provided by DESY.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but are assumed to be independent of direction. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order partial differential equation is developed, which includes all terms from a two-layer model based on the Prandtl-Blasius approximation, effectively disregarding certain weak terms. This model is analyzed within the context of a boundary-layer approximation and its equations are singularly perturbed. Using the WKB approximation method, an approach that incorporates an abrupt change is utilized to find solutions near points of singularity. Additionally, a comprehensive survey of related literature is included. The study demonstrates that under specific conditions, solutions display oscillatory behavior over extended intervals and, in certain contexts, this oscillatory nature can be eliminated, leading to improved approximations of the original partial differential equation. Specifically, when certain spatial and temporal conditions are met, a quasilinear second-order equation is derived, effectively describing the vertical velocity component as a product of boundary-layer corrections multiplied by a function of the independent variables, which in certain instances can be simplified to match the physical optics approximation. The study also explores alternatives to this physical optics approximation, incorporating both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors into a simplified first-order equation. The results demonstrate that, although the physical optics approximation may not always be applicable, its inclusion can provide insight into the nature of solutions and help refine boundary conditions. Furthermore, the study analyzes the spatial development of turbulence, influencing velocity profiles in different regions of the flow and revealing how various parameters contribute to its spatial development. The study also examines the temporal development of turbulence and its interaction with both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, influencing velocity profiles in different regions of the flow. The results demonstrate that an approach combining all terms of the model, including those not included in the physical optics approximation, provides a more complete understanding of both the spatial and temporal development of turbulence. The study also includes a discussion on how the singular perturbation nature of the model, effective only near points of singularity, contributes to the development of turbulence and highlights the importance of considering all terms in the model to accurately predict turbulence development. The study effectively encompasses both the physical optics approximation and the complete model, emphasizing the dependence on directional viscosity factors and specific spatial and temporal conditions to accurately predict velocity profiles in different regions of the flow. A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects. Existing reinforcement learning systems focus primarily on optimizing target acquisition but often neglect to account for the inherent uncertainty associated with visual observations. Drawing from information theory, our approach aims to balance target proximity with the desire to gather more informative visual data, thereby reducing uncertainty. We demonstrated the efficacy of our method through numerical experiments involving synthetic environments with varying levels of complexity and real-world navigation challenges utilizing RGB-D and pointcloud data. For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which asymptotically flat spacetimes become singular at infinity are significantly more complex and highly dependent on the spacetime's description. In general, it is found that the Bondi mass change rate is proportional to the spacetime's energy density, which may be positive or negative. In the case of spherically symmetric black holes, the mass change rate is found to be directly influenced by the accretion rate and is subject to specific constraints determined by the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkov equation. Using a graphical analysis in the $\rho-A$ plane, the possible range of accretion rates is mapped out for several asymptotically flat spacetimes, including Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordstrom, and charged dilaton black holes. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and, within these clusters, 43% of the originals will have merged by z=6.5. This includes a substantial number of mergers that produce gravitational waves detectable by LISA, with 53% of these instances occurring at redshifts between 6.5 and 8. In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel method using system-wide pattern seeking capabilities to develop performance models for ESS and differential current detectors. These models are then combined to create an optimized algorithm for identifying abnormal operating conditions in the controlled flow of current. Simulation tests conducted on the standard IEEE 33-node distribution network, where realistic usage patterns are applied, show that the proposed method is capable of detecting multiple incident scenarios, including malfunctioning ESS and faulty protective devices. Following a detailed discussion on implementation limitations, this method can be integrated with the control system and communication infrastructure to provide the distribution system operator with real-time data on malfunctions, system performance, and energy usage. This information can then be used to refine control policies and improve the overall efficiency of the distribution network. The proposed solution leverages the capabilities of the advanced digital control system to offer a cost-effective solution for malfunction detection. By utilizing existing digital infrastructure, this solution eliminates the need for additional hardware or sensors. Furthermore, this method does not disrupt the functioning of the protection system, as it does not rely on overload or current-related parameters to operate. Finally, this solution can be adapted for use in other applications beyond power distribution networks, and can be characterized by its simplicity. We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces. Additionally, by employing the concept of derived categories of curves, we establish that not all quadrics can be deformed into one another. Furthermore, under certain conditions, the quadrics that can be deformed into each other form a finite number and are parameterized by the Picard number of the initial quadric. If the quadric contains a rational curve, then the quadrics that can be deformed into each other are those associated with the tensor products of the initial quadric and a specific finite number of hyperplane line bundles. Also, when the quadric has the property that its tangent space is isomorphic to the tensor product of one linear space and the quadric's fundamental line bundle, then the quadrics that can be deformed into each other are those given by the tensor products of the initial quadric and a specific finite number of external tensor products of the linear space and the quadric. We provide a list that specifies the deformations of the quadrics of dimensions two, three, and four. We also conjecture that this finiteness property holds for all quadrics and, as evidence, provide a list that specifies the deformations of the quadrics containing a plane. The text also contains numerous open problems and conjectures. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than several days or even weeks. 
Our study employs one million steps as the new standard for comprehensive evaluations, compares the performance of four virtual agents under this new benchmark, and finds that their skills improve significantly in the optimized environment. 
Our agents not only solve problems more efficiently, but also exhibit enhanced language skills, solving a higher percentage of problems in the new game environment. 
Finally, we propose a novel performance metric that evaluates an agent's overall capability to apply its knowledge across a wide range of text-based challenges. 
Our study demonstrates that leading agents can now be evaluated in a comprehensive way within a single day, paving the way for more effective training and a greater potential for breakthroughs in natural language processing, problem solving, and other areas. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/TextWorld/textworld-express. 
Our website, https://textworldexpress.github.io, offers a simple online interface for running your own text-based challenges at high processing speeds and tracks the performance of virtual agents over time. Our research follows standard ethical guidelines for AI research as outlined in Kerr et al. (2018), ensuring that our study does not pose significant risks to human subjects. Our website also provides an online tutorial for new users, explaining the rules of three widely used text-based game challenges in a comprehensive and easy-to-understand format. Our optimization technique is freely available as a Python package on GitHub at https://github.com/flashest/textworld, offering a wide range of customizable options for simulating text games. Our study employs a rigorous, evidence-based approach to identify the key technology components that are most worthy of further attention. Our website also offers an interactive tool for conducting empirical studies, allowing researchers to examine the effect of our new game environment on virtual agents in a comprehensive way. The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. However, this study investigates spin defects which, being disordered, shouldn't influence the shift according to conventional geometry. We disagree with this conventional understanding and have developed a model involving spin-1/2 particles on a honeycomb lattice with a chiral gap, incorporating impurities that break time-reversal symmetry. The imposed potential due to these impurities generates a unique magnetic field in momentum space, causing a spin orientation shift within the zone. The shift is proportional to the geometric tensor's imaginary part, thereby validating our unconventional approach. Moreover, we find that this geometric tensor is proportional to the SU(4) tensor constructed from the spinor wave function's second covariant derivative. We propose that this proportionality serves as a practical criterion to identify Topological Insulators with defects. We have developed a practical algorithm to calculate the geometric tensor, thereby providing a practical method to identify Topological Insulators with defects. The novel approach outlined here has the potential to be adapted and used in various problems involving particle defects. We have also developed a quantum circuit model of the system which can be used to investigate the holographic properties of the system as well as its quantum thermodynamic properties. The circuit, comprising an entangling gate driven by the geometric tensor, is shown to be equivalent to a SU(2) rotation driven by the tensor's imaginary part, thereby facilitating the development of a quantum algorithm to identify Topological Insulators with defects. We have extended this approach to systems described by higher-dimensional Riemannian manifolds and have developed a universal algorithm to identify Topological Insulators with defects. The algorithm employs a gauge field that can be represented by a spinor wave function, thereby facilitating the development of a quantum circuit model of the system. The circuit, comprising a sequence of entangling gates, is shown to be equivalent to a SU(2) rotation driven by the Riemannian tensor's imaginary part, thereby controlling the shift in electron spin orientation within the zone. The circuit's ergodicity, coupled with the fact that the geometric tensor's eigenvalues are either real or conjugate, provides a practical method to identify Topological Insulators with defects. The novel approach outlined here has the potential to be adapted and used in various problems involving particle defects as well as devices based on spin orientation shifts. The development of this approach is a significant breakthrough in the field of quantum physics

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a new method to transfer manipulability information from one robot to another with a different kinematic structure. Since these ellipsoids are based on symmetric positive-definite matrices, they can be treated as points on a specific geometric manifold. This work offers the first approach to transfer manipulability by leveraging the technique of point cloud registration. To achieve this, it employs an algorithm combining parallel transport with Iterative Closest Point. The method also uses an adaptive geometric matching heuristic to improve alignment results. To evaluate its effectiveness, it conducts experiments involving robotic systems with various configurations and also incorporates human demonstrations in manipulability transfer for the first time. The findings of these experiments show the method's high degree of accuracy and its ability to achieve close original performance on complex manipulators. The developed approach is now available online. This research has been documented by a video available at https://youtu.be/1U8U6C0T4Hk. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/frc-mlts-publications/hrm-manipulability-tda. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by a model for predicting object poses in a single view. In contrast to existing top-tier models, this method performs competitively without relying on explicit 3D pose annotations during the training process. Additionally, we present the Accidental Turntables Dataset, a set of challenging images depicting 41,212 car scenarios with complex backgrounds, motion blur, and varying lighting conditions, serving as a new benchmark for 3D pose estimation. Our method's superiority is demonstrated through benchmark experiments on three and four views, as well as with the new Accidental Turntables Dataset. Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current approaches. Experiments were conducted on the recently created CoVaxLies dataset, a comprehensive collection of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation gathered from Twitter discussions. This new dataset allows us to distinguish which specific types of misinformation are more commonly accepted and which are more commonly disputed. Our analysis shows that tweets acknowledging the risk involved are more likely to be disseminated, whereas those emphasizing benefits are less likely to be shared. This research may contribute to developing strategies aimed at mitigating the dissemination of misinformation. A related issue is the distinction between various forms of misinformation, such as "benefit-focused" and "risk-focused," which we later intend to explore in relation to our findings. Our expected contribution is two-fold: first, we would identify the dissemination stance, second, we would learn to classify misinformation types. This study could yield valuable insights for developers creating anti-disinformation systems and may facilitate efforts to encourage the dissemination of accurate information. Moreover, our work could assist in framing countermeasures aimed specifically at mitigating the spread of misinformation emphasizing potential vaccine benefits. Conversely, our results could be instrumental in guiding endeavors to discourage the dissemination of misinformation highlighting risks. It is our hope that the frameworks and approaches outlined here could facilitate efforts to control the dissemination of various types of misinformation. This work is comprised of two distinct parts. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths. Moreover, we propose that by employing electronic coherence, it's theoretically possible to achieve unprecedented levels of temporal and spatial confinement. These advancements can be applied across multiple areas of attosecond science and accelerated material production, potentially expanding our knowledge to the femtosecond timescale. Lastly, we acknowledge that our model relies on a semi-classical framework, but waveform synthesis can be effectively used to create harmonic spectra and electron momentum distributions with significant quantitative agreement, despite the inherent limitations posed by the magnitude of electric fields generated by harmonic generation. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This modification, which is inspired by a technique proposed by Burtnyk and Holmer, essentially dispenses with the physical domain's influence on the proof. Furthermore, we derive a new estimate of the second derivative of the modified variance, which is crucial for controlling the boundary terms. We also introduce a novel approach, inspired by the well-known nonlinear Schrödinger equation's conservation laws, to bound the solutions' real part within a suitable Sobolev space. This technique, which is independently applicable and valuable in its own right, allows us to derive a Strichartz inequality for solutions in this exterior domain scenario. The proof itself is a intricate combination of the established conservation laws and the modified variance method. Lastly, we address solutions with positive energy by applying similar techniques, along with a strategy first introduced by Roudenko, which leverages the well-posedness of a related linear equation in a large domain. The latter part of the paper relies on a conservation law for the solutions' Hamiltonian, which was first demonstrated by Roudenko, as well as a novel time-weighted inequality measure. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods. Notably, our approach outperforms existing techniques under no/few boundary value conditions, while achieving comparable results when combined with existing techniques. Furthermore, we provide theoretical analysis that explains its performance from a high-level perspective. To facilitate broader use, we also release related code on an openly-accessed platform. Overall, our approach makes a significant contribution to improving the efficiency of physics-informed neural networks. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing attacks, our method doesn't rely on a specific model or rely on the target model's parameters, and it doesn't need a pair of corresponding images, instead relying on the semantic relationship between them. Our method uses a neural network that can distinguish between the natural and man-made features of objects, and it is difficult to evade detection by classification models, especially those that rely on natural objects. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method through an experiment in which human annotators were asked to label object classes without realizing that the labels would be used for a Trojan attack. The result is near-perfect classification of the target model's labels, and the attack can be adapted to classify other models on the same dataset with even higher accuracy. Our method is particularly challenging to detect because it can be adapted to classify key events in various applications, such as video, without affecting the visual content. Additionally, it can be employed in speech without altering the audio content. We have released the code for our method on GitHub under the MIT License, along with the annotated dataset. We believe that semantic Trojan attacks can serve as a significant threat to machine learning models in practical use cases. We see this attack method as a double-edged sword, posing a significant risk of being exploited, but also providing valuable insights for improving the robustness of machine learning models against such threats. In particular, it highlights the potential for attackers to manipulate models by exploiting differences in object classes, and it reveals the difficulty of developing effective defense mechanisms, particularly those that rely on natural object classes. Ultimately, we see this Trojan attack method as a means of educating the machine learning community about the potential for semantic attacks and providing a framework for testing the robustness of models against such threats. In the future, we will focus on developing semantic Trojan attacks that utilize subtle changes in object classes, and we will also explore the feasibility of employing natural object classes in Trojan attacks. Furthermore, we will investigate new approaches to detecting semantic Trojan attacks that take into account the semantic relationships between objects, such as using generative adversarial networks to detect attacks based on the similarity between natural and man-made object classes. Finally, we will work on developing effective defense mechanisms, such as training models to be robust against subtle changes in object classes, and providing a framework for testing the robustness of models against semantic Trojan attacks. We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 2000 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient examination of expansive astronomical objects like nebulae and galaxies. Our system will permit the simultaneous examination of extended objects at four distinct spectral intervals, thereby significantly decreasing sky subtraction time. In addition to being an IMACS upgrade, ROSIE IFU will also be compatible with the Keck II HIRES spectrograph for comparative studies. Our goal is to have the system installed and the first observations conducted by the end of 2008. We will present the results of our first observations, which will be conducted during the commissioning of the Magellan Baade Telescope, in an upcoming follow-up paper. Our calculations indicate that ROSIE IFU will significantly boost the observation efficiency for various astronomical objects. For instance, it will permit the rapid gathering of 10 to the power of 5 distinct spectra with a resolution of 2000, in a single 10 hour night, by dividing the Lyman continuum spectrum into 1000 sections. This represents a 10 fold increase in productivity compared to two spectrum sections, as previously achieved through earlier experiments. Similarly, in a single 10 hour night, we will be able to collect an enormous 10 to the power of 6 "doublet spectra" with a 0.3 Angstrom separation, thereby substantially expanding the existing database. Our calculations indicate that this enormous database could be utilized to substantially expand our present understanding of various astronomical objects like galaxies and nebulae. Furthermore, this enormous database could also be used to significantly expand our present understanding of various stellar spectra. A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying the type of celestial body they are.  If an exoplanet's parent star has similar elemental composition to our Sun, it may not be a terrestrial body, as these planets typically form around G-type dwarfs with Sun-like composition.  However, the problem arises in cases where we do not know the elemental composition of the parent star.  In such situations, analyzing the abundance of a planet's host star can provide insights into the possible internal composition of the exoplanet.  Drawing from a database of 26 proven planetary hosts, this study utilizes a sophisticated model to examine various relationships between a star and its terrestrial planet, incorporating factors such as the star's metallicity, the planet's mass, and its orbit.  The results indicate that in systems containing super-Earths and Neptune-mass planets, the stars tend to be richer in metals compared to the Sun.  Furthermore, the study reveals connections between a star's properties and the possible internal compositions of its planetary companion, suggesting that planets with a mass of less than three times that of Earth are likely composed of iron and silicate rocks.  Conversely, more massive planets may be primarily made up of iron.  The analysis also suggests that planets as large as two to three times the size of Earth in a 100-day orbit around G-type stars are likely composed of equal parts iron and silicate rocks.  The findings of this research may be useful in planning future studies of exoplanet internal structures, as they are likely to be a focus of high priority in upcoming research.  The data analyzed in this study have been made publicly available, and the code used for the analysis can be accessed at a designated website. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN. Additionally, the proposed solution facilitates better feature interpretation through attention weights. By concentrating network capacity on critical channels, the need for extensive channel recording throughout the training process can be eliminated, thereby accelerating training. The support rates of the top N channels in two railway scenarios are found to be 93.7% and 88.3%, respectively. As a result, the proposed system can be efficiently deployed in real-world scenarios with complex channel conditions. Experimental results indicate that the localization error is reduced by 14% across two test scenarios with significantly fewer channel recordings, thereby enhancing overall localization efficiency. The computational complexity of the proposed approach is determined and found to be comparable to that of a conventional DNN. The time required for data recording is significantly lower, from 365.6 sec to 10.1 sec. The correlation between attention weights and channel power is investigated and found to be substantial, thereby enabling attention weights to effectively act as feature interpreters for CSI. The relevance of individual channels to localization is accurately captured by the attention weights. As a result, the proposed approach can be reliably applied to locate devices in real-world scenarios with complex channel conditions by focusing on a manageable number of critical channels. Moreover, the localisation error can be minimised by reducing the number of channels recorded during training, and this reduction is directly linked to the attention weights. Consequently, the proposed approach is expected to contribute to the efficient application of wireless localisation systems. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic by linking different types of logical semantics together. Based on an expansion of the original modal logic's semantic structure, we can translate one category to another, preserving the meaning. We demonstrate that the topological category is the most comprehensive framework, containing all other categories as subcategories. This framework offers a unified approach to modal logic, empowering us to compare and analyze the semantic structures of various logics within a standardized system. This is the first installment of a two-part series; the follow-up paper will delve into the algebraic aspects of this unified system. We will also apply this framework to investigate the semantic structure of hybrid logics. Specifically, we will show that the topological category is equivalent to the category of complete Priestley spaces when applied to S5, and that the subcategory consisting of Priestley spaces is a natural extension of the original modal logic. Furthermore, we will define a specific hybrid logic as a system that extends S5 by incorporating the syntax related to the fibre, a concept introduced by the researcher G. G. Waldhoff, effectively making it equivalent to the topological modal logic based on the Priestley spaces. This hybrid logic emerges as a natural extension of the original modal logic as well as S5. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In scenarios where n is less than the sum of i and j, but with a sufficiently large alphabet size of at least 4, we identify similar properties of functions. In particular, we establish a characterization for the functions within the eigenspace U_i(n,q) with minimum possible support in several specific scenarios. In addition, we identify and prove a theorem relating to orthogonal projections onto eigenspaces of the Hamming graphs. As a byproduct of our study, we make notable observations on certain function properties, including their identities, distributions, and Hamming norms. We also make a connection between our results and Zinoviev's work on balls within the Hamming graphs. Throughout the paper, we use a combination of tools, including graph theory and the theory of finite geometries. We also utilize weight enumerators to analyze and understand the structures of the functions in question. In particular, we make use of Draper and Ward's work on identifying and describing the possible structures of the functions in question. Our study is motivated by a long-standing question regarding the identifiability of and/or/Xor codes proposed by Ashikhmin. We also make a connection between our result and a conjecture by Vilenkin. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI. Under development are a web-based model sharing feature and an interface for sharing model simulations, both featuring Google Collab as a pre-configured environment. Ultimately, ShinyCOPASI will bridge the gap between web-based educational resources and the full capabilities of COPASI. To facilitate educational efforts, we also introduced 'COPASI Byte-Sized', a series of brief tutorials demonstrating ShinyCOPASI's capabilities. You can find these educational tools on the COPASI wiki at https://copasi.org/educational_tools. Additionally, we published a publication outlining the technical details of ShinyCOPASI, available on bioRxiv at https://dx.doi.org/10.1101/2022.07.11.21260655. We expect ShinyCOPASI to broaden COPASI's accessibility and enhance the platform's features. It will be essential in educational initiatives due to its user-friendly and exploratory interface, making it a valuable tool for educational purposes in biochemistry and systems biology. Furthermore, we anticipate ShinyCOPASI to be a versatile platform for various applications, such as web-based educational resources and research tools. To demonstrate ShinyCOPASI's potential in educational settings, we created three 'Byte-Sized' tutorials covering its core capabilities. You can access these tutorials on the COPASI wiki at https://copasi.org/educational_tools. Moving forward, we will continue developing ShinyCOPASI by incorporating user feedback and expanding its features to make it an indispensable tool for systems biology research and education. We achieved this by publishing the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI and providing a detailed technical description at https://dx.doi.org/10.1101/2022.07.11.212606

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library. In a subsequent study, we will leverage this framework to develop novel methods and refine existing techniques. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to the development of a reliable and robust tradition of solving PDEs with NNs. This work is a direct result of three years spent studying and working on UQ in NNs, culminating in a doctoral dissertation. In a companion paper, we plan to explore the numerical approximation properties of NNs. As an open-source community, we welcome contributions of all kinds and encourage you to join the conversation. Please feel free to contact us by email at [uqnn@umich.edu](uqnn@umich.edu). We look forward to hearing from you! A public discussion thread on this research is also available at https://www.reddit.com/r/MachineLearning/comments/m0s70b/uncertainty_quantification_in_scientific_machine?

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees. Inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms standard policy iteration by achieving a better contraction rate and reduced computational expense. Moreover, inexact GMRES policy iteration can also be applied to large-scale continuous MDPs under weakened assumptions. Numerical examples showcase the efficiency of inexact GMRES policy iteration. In particular, it outperforms standard policy iteration by at least one order of magnitude in a traffic management case study. A C implementation is available online at https://github.com/fredyabraham/inexact-gmres-policy-iteration. In addition, an open-source Python package, SCS, includes inexact GMRES policy iteration as of version 8.1.3. This package may be downloaded at https://github.com/cran/cran/blob/master/DESCRIPTION. Furthermore, inexact GMRES policy iteration has been integrated into PyRoocs under version 2.0.2 as a module called inexact_policy_iteration. This module may be downloaded at https://github.com/muscoe/PyRoocs. inexact GMRES policy iteration can also be incorporated into any Python code through pip installation of the PyRoocs package. A Python code snippet is available online at https://github.com/fredyabraham/inexact-gmres-policy-iteration. In addition, inexact GMRES policy iteration has been successfully applied to at least two other problems. Specifically, it was used by Yale and Harvard researchers to solve a problem involving the management of Yale's and Harvard's combined parking facilities. In a separate study, it was also employed by researchers from the laboratory for joint dynamics to solve a multi-robot motion planning problem. Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example generation, but almost no restrictions are necessary for the reliable learnability of simple models. We investigate the boundary between these two scenarios by studying the learnability of halfspaces under the influence of example noise and limited feedback. Specifically, we demonstrate that certain distributional assumptions are necessary to guarantee the reliable learnability of halfspaces when the number of available labels is very few, but almost no restrictions are necessary when the number of available labels is significant. Notably, our results reveal the importance of local queries in the learning process, as using global queries would lead to a significant decrease in the robustness margin. Additionally, we utilize a novel distribution to showcase a scenario in which the robustness margin is infinitely small, even when using local queries, and this scenario cannot be bypassed by using global queries. Finally, we combine our findings on robust learning and active learning to establish a new boundary between these two scenarios. The boundary we obtained is shown to be sharp, and specific theoretical and practical considerations for achieving this boundary were also examined. Lastly, as an experimental validation of our theoretical findings, we developed and tested the Local-Feedback-Query (LFQ) algorithm, an efficient and effective algorithm for learning robust halfspaces that combines the benefits of local queries and the ability to obtain multiple labels. The LFQ algorithm was shown to be significantly faster and more accurate than the robust empirical risk minimization method. Moreover, the LFQ algorithm was found to be comparable to the passive learning approach that doesn't consider example noise. The code for the LFQ algorithm is available on GitHub. Lastly, we identified promising directions for further research. The LFQ algorithm was found to be ineffective when dealing with more complex models, and it didn't perform well under specific distributional assumptions. The main difficulty was to determine the optimal trade-off between the influence of example noise and the influence of limited feedback, and we overcame this difficulty by utilizing a new regularization term that is specifically designed to handle this trade-off.
