Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time options, such as input parameters, allowing users to modify them to fulfill different purposes, such as reducing the system's footprint or improving security, yet these configurations often go unused in a specific system instance. In our research, we devised an experimental approach to reduce a system's configurable parameters during compilation, eliminating unnecessary settings on a per-class basis, by analyzing the system's source code, thus streamlining the system's run-time configuration space. Our method was evaluated on the SSHD benchmark suite and four open-source applications from the cybersecurity domain, where we found that around 64% of a system's run-time configuration space can be specialized at compile-time, yielding up to a 40% decrease in the system's binary size and around 1.4% average performance improvement. Moreover, we discovered that a substantial portion, approximately 80%, of the system's accessible input parameters can be eliminated from the system's binary, thus potentially preventing malicious actors from exploiting them in attack scenarios. This research lays the groundwork for future developments in software configuration management. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI estimation as a significant area of focus. Recent breakthroughs have involved the use of deep learning, which has improved signal quality and diagnostic accuracy, although existing methods still have room for improvement. A new study introduces a ground-breaking technique based on a Tiramisu autoencoder that surpasses previous estimates of error, achieving an impressive 0.0098 $m/s^2$ in PDD, a measure of accuracy in estimating heart rate. This advancement is attributed to two key features of the model: Densely-Connected Neural Networks and a Novel Loss Function, which together increase the training efficiency and accuracy of the algorithm. As a result, the same researchers were inspired to develop a wearable ECG device, which demonstrates the data-driven benefits of their invention. Experimental data collected from 76 subjects, representing a diverse range of ages and activities, further affirm the excellence of their model. Notably, the new technique has shown remarkable performance on data from the FSPIEOG dataset, a benchmark used to evaluate signal processing, and has even surpassed previous results by 3.6%. This cutting-edge model is now being translated into a software tool, referred to as TiramisWatch, which is set to revolutionize the field of wearable ECG devices. As such, the study has potential applications in remote health monitoring and will pave the way for the development of more advanced, deep-learning-based ECG devices. By leveraging this model, healthcare services can be made more accessible, reducing the need for costly hospital visits and procedures. In effect, the study is a significant step toward achieving a more distributed, resource-poor model of healthcare. We analyze large deviations of power input by an active force on an Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Particle (AOUP) within or outside a confinement. Analytical calculations of the rate function are done for the free particle in any dimension using a saddle-point expansion. Additionally, a direct numerical approach via solution of the AOUP equations is performed, alongside a method using Legendre-Fenchel transform of the scaled cumulant generating function obtained via a cloning algorithm. Results for the free particle exhibit asymptotically linear behavior on both sides, dependent on a multiplicative factor of the dimension. Conversely, confinement scenarios in two dimensions display distinct behavior when applying active force in either harmonic or anharmonic potentials, each exhibiting varying rate function and mechanism. Moreover, a fluctuation relation for active work distribution is verified in free particles, exhibiting temperature-dependent behavior. Similar verification occurs in cases involving harmonic potential, while in anharmonic cases, verification holds at low active force levels; yet at high levels of active force in anharmonic cases, a distinct effective temperature, derived from the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, is found to govern behavior. This research provides comprehensive insight into the nature of active motion within both confined and free environments, aligning with recent experiments involving active colloids. Furthermore, this study paves the way for applying large deviation techniques in analyzing active matter, potentially extending to scenarios involving even more complex systems. Lastly, the observed patterns of large active work fluctuations, associated with high and low effective temperatures, may be viewed as a form of active Brownian ratchet, providing a theoretical basis for understanding observed, active motor behaviors in experiments. These findings can potentially be applied and translated into technical innovations, such as the development of artificial active matter that could be used to create innovative technologies. Lastly, this study also provides a theoretical basis for understanding and analyzing active biological cells, which exhibit intricate movements facilitated by molecular motors due to having an active force incorporated within their mechanics. Therefore, this study not only aligns with experimental findings but also provides a theoretical basis for understanding and analyzing both artificial and living matter. It is anticipated that the technical innovations resulting from this research will lead to the creation of ground-breaking technology. Lastly, this theoretical basis for understanding active matter may also lead to the development of new therapeutic methods. Additionally, we speculate that our theoretical findings may also lead to the creation of new and innovative sporting equipment. These potential applications are directly attributed to the unique properties of active matter, which can now be comprehensively analyzed via the theoretical basis provided by this study.

We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages, comparing it to other leading cross-lingual transfer methods and traditional from-scratch training techniques. Our results demonstrate that our method can achieve comparable or even better performance with much less data, and up to a 5% improvement in certain settings with a full dataset. You can find our code and data here: https://github.com/jacey-lyu/NTRT. Our findings suggest that weak supervision can significantly streamline neural model translation, making it a promising prospect for reducing the costs associated with developing natural language processing applications in under-resourced languages. In particular, neural task representations serve as an efficient and language-independent means of conveying the required information for model translation. By combining this with model agnostic approaches to handling data differences and a straightforward fine-tuning process, we've created a translation protocol that's both model and language-agnostic. Our work has the potential to increase the accessibility of neural models for tasks such as sentiment analysis, leading to a broader range of applications across more languages. Furthermore, the success of our approach in the NLP domain could inspire similar innovations in other machine learning tasks. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the scale factor. A broadly applicable geometric proof has demonstrated that the maximum efficiency in these systems can be achieved by alternating between the maximum and minimum permissible temperatures and scale factor values. For situations where the scale factor range is restricted and the system's thermal state closely matches its equilibrium values at temperature plateaus, this protocol also ensures maximum output energy production. These findings are valid for a wide range of physical systems, including an overdamped heat engine driven by a particle in an optical tweezers setup characterized by a scale factor related to the stiffness. We have also developed an analytical solution for an underdamped oscillator heat engine and compared its performance with that of a traditionally controlled quantum spin-bath system, highlighting the potential for significant improvements. Furthermore, we have defined a set of protocol-dependent fundamental limits that relate the system's characteristic energy to the scale factor and the detailed balance condition, thereby providing a valuable framework for the optimization of heat engines in a variety of practical contexts. Finally, we have explored the protocol's potential for a wide range of systems, also known as Brownian ratchets, and identified the underlying principle as a time-dependent variation in the system's dynamics, which can be controlled to produce work through the coordination of thermal fluctuations. This concept is expected to extend beyond the realm of thermodynamics and could be applied in a variety of fields to optimize the performance of sequential control systems. It is also noteworthy that this work is related to another recent study on the application of sequential control to quantum systems, which could be the subject of further joint research and collaborative development. Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels. In this article, we take a comprehensive approach to explore various scalar models, with a primary focus on the naturalness of electroweak symmetry breaking and the properties of scalar particles, while also considering the accessibility of models through various signatures and experimental detection possibilities. Furthermore, we examine how the experiments' sensitivity evolves with increasing collider energy. Although this article concentrates on the most widely-debated naturalness issues, it is essential to note that there are additional concerns where the scalar sector may differ from the Standard Model, such as the top quark's properties or the dark matter scenario. A thorough analysis of all these matters is a complex task and is the subject of ongoing research, with consideration of various cases and models presented here. These models include the two-Higgs-Doublet model (2HDM), the minimal R-parity violating supersymmetric model (MRPSVM), the non-supersymmetric universal extra dimensions model (model I of the UED model), the D-brane motivated string local model, the little Higgs with T-parity model, and the anomalous U(1) model. We provide a comprehensive review of these models, along with a detailed analysis of the experimental detection possibilities, the potential signatures, and the proposed searches that could be conducted in future collider experiments. In particular, our specific analysis concerns the rate of the Higgs boson's production and its subsequent self-coupling, the characteristics of additional scalar bosons, and the properties of scalar matter particles. Lastly, this article also discusses the required energy for the collider that can detect all the scalar particles in a comprehensive theoretical model. A thorough comparison with other existing studies on the same models has been included [1,2]. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum by comparing active to quiet periods. By using SDO imagery, we quantified the proportion of active areas (faculae and spots) on the solar surface, independent of previous activity indicators. These features were linked to variations in solar faculae coverage, as observed on the visible hemisphere of the Sun. Moreover, the spectral features were observed to shift towards longer wavelengths as the star's active regions rotate into view. These patterns were consistent across two separate data sets and the spectral features showed correlations with the star's activity characteristics, making them potential indicators of a star's magnetic behavior. These indicators may provide valuable insights for analyzing observations of other stars, potentially improving the detection of exoplanets. Based on our analysis, which accounted for potential measurement errors, all these indicators appear reliable for analyzing stellar activity and searching for exoplanets on active stars. However, the spectral features could be improved by using data from higher angular resolutions and better signal-to-noise ratios. These potential activity indicators can now be studied in other active stars observed by other telescopes to verify their utility in analyzing observations of these stars. Additionally, these indicators could be used to analyze other data sets, including those from the Kepler and TESS missions, to explore their applicability on a larger scale. If applicable, these indicators could be used to correct for the star's activity signals and improve the detection of exoplanets. To facilitate this, we have made our analyzed data available on a public platform. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero energies in the tunneling spectra of topological superconductors, particularly in presence of Ohmic dissipation, we investigate using a spectroscopic approach employing resistive gates. This approach is grounded in the fact that realistic gate devices are expected to exhibit some degree of dissipation. The tunneling current through a superconductor is governed by its density of states, which has two distinct behaviors in the presence of topological superconductors: a zero-bias peak which could be fragmented due to dissipation and a characteristic peak at a finite energy due to a localized Andreev reflection. The presence of Ohmic dissipation causes the zero-bias peak to become fragmented into two peaks at zero and a finite energy, distinguishable from the topological superconductor's characteristic peak. The proposed method hinges on the distinction in the spectral features produced by Ohmic dissipation. The resilience of the spectral features to varying dissipation strengths and the variability in gate height were assessed through numerical simulations using a scattering-regime model. The results indicate that the proposed spectroscopic technique based on resistive gates is an effective means of identifying Majorana zero-energy peaks distinguishable from those at non-zero energies in the tunneling spectra of topological superconductors. The technique is expected to be effective even in the presence of disorder and other scenarios characterized by high dissipation. The implementation of this method could significantly contribute to the search for Majorana zero-energy peaks in topological superconductors. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes with no definitive measure of their correctness. While target images can be created using numerical methods, the process usually involves an iterative, trial-and-error process due to the difficulty in determining appropriate control values. To streamline this process, we propose a novel neural network architecture that learns to distill a desirable style from paired images, allowing it to be applied consistently across a wide range of input images. By double backtracking the control values, the network enforces smooth and predictable behavior. The distilled style can then be utilized through an optimized sampling process, eliminating the need for manual control value setting. The efficacy of this approach was demonstrated through various image editing tasks including color timing, black and white conversion, and splashing. The code for these experiments is publicly available at https://github.com/zzarzy/style_distillation. Additionally, a demo showcasing the neural network's performance can be found at https://zzarzy.github.io/style_distillation/. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method excels at producing targeted images while being insensitive to initial control values, unlike other approaches. Moreover, the style distillation network displays remarkable generalization capabilities on unseen images, surpassing other comparable methods. The proposed approach significantly streamlines the image editing process, significantly reducing the number of manual control values required to produce a targeted image. Moreover, the network's ability to capture a consistent style across paired images opens up new avenues for image representation. The method's code will be publicly available shortly. This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is significantly affected, leading to the concentration of larger snowflakes in the upper layers of snowdrifts. Large snowflakes are observed to move preferentially towards the direction of air flow turbulence at velocities up to 1.5 times their normal falling speed. This phenomenon provides a potential mechanism for the self-organization of unique snow patterns observed in certain atmospheric conditions. A newly introduced metric, the sweepiness parameter $\La$, is proposed to quantify the balance between preferential sweeping and random settling, yielding a unique value for the atmosphere, with further modeling and simulation needed to fully understand this process. Our study provides invaluable insights for modeling atmospheric deposition and can be applied to other similar systems. Moreover, this research has significant practical implications for ski slope management, snow road maintenance, and aviation safety. By analyzing our data in the range of the Eulerian scale, we detected large-scale vortex formations above the ground, driving snowflake settling towards specific areas, leading to uneven snow distribution. A comparative study of our results with previous numerical modeling studies is also presented. A new class of lagrangian models is proposed to capture the essence of preferential sweeping, providing a valuable contribution to the scientific community. The findings of this study can be freely accessed and utilized. Additionally, we have made available a detailed guide to reconstruct the data, allowing other researchers to replicate and build upon our findings. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. While still in its early stages, this work shows that sophisticated mental frameworks powered by deep learning can enable a robotic system to generate relevant predictions and facilitate a meaningful hypothesis-testing process. Experimentation involves a robotic system navigating an unfamiliar office environment, with the findings indicating that active inference can be exploited to create a self-referential, mentally-generated map of the surroundings. This research paves the way for the development of sophisticated mental systems powered by deep learning, enabling advanced agents to seamlessly integrate navigation and other essential tasks within a unified, theoretically-sound framework. In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. However, the data sets generated in these fields typically comprise of vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods like Gzip and LZO tend to be inefficient. Furthermore, most existing sparse data compression approaches have been confined to specific dimensions, hindering their generalizability across various domains. To address these challenges, a cutting-edge sparse data compression technique referred to as Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), is being developed in collaboration between InftySigns and the CPPM, as part of the LHCb's TPC renewal project. The innovative BCAE approach leverages the principles of 3D sparse data compression, distinct value distribution, and training-based customization to break through the limitations of traditional compression methods. The efficacy of BCAE was tested across various custom sparsity patterns and value distributions and was found to outperform the industry-standard Gzip and LZO compression methods by a significant margin, achieving up to 42% better compression rates, along with an average reduction in data transfer volumes of approximately 31%. The outstanding performance of BCAE makes it an attractive solution for the efficient compression of large 3D sparse data volumes in a wide range of real-world applications. The code base for this project is openly accessible on GitHub. The development and customization of BCAE for specific use cases can be facilitated through the provided API, along with a comprehensive Python package that includes pre-trained models and a range of auxiliary tools. The computational framework employed in this research was provided by InftySigns, a novel, bicephalous architecture consisting of two cognitive modules: the code predictor and the value predictor. The latter is capable of accurately forecasting data values based on specific spatial and temporal patterns, effectively eliminating the need for repeated data transmission or storage. The code predictor identifies and transmits only the unique indices of significant data values, allowing the remaining zeros to be automatically filled in at the reception end. The efficacy of this approach was validated through numerous comprehensive studies and is being successfully applied in the LHCb's TPC renewal project. A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing strides can be 14% longer than the Pacific Lamprey's, making this innovative design a promising approach for robots navigating steep surfaces with limited support points. This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework. Doxorubicin and IL-2 synergistic effects also emerge from the simulations, showcasing the potential for higher tumor reduction when administered together, as opposed to the treatments being used individually. The introduced framework can streamline the process of identifying optimal combinations of treatments. The direct linkage between control policies and probability distributions allows the analysis of various probabilistic outcomes associated with distinct control policies, thus enabling the identification of treatments with concurrent benefits and adverse effects. Consequently, the probabilistic model can guide the search for the most effective combination of treatments by initially focusing on those with desired outcomes and excluding those with adverse effects. The direct calculation of probability distributions may prove impractical for more complex systems; however, the introduced framework's approach based on machine learning can be employed to identify optimal treatment combinations through deep reinforcement learning. The resulting learning model can then be utilized to predict the colon cancer dynamics trajectory in response to any given treatment combination. The predicted probability distribution also enables the estimation of tumor reduction and adverse effects associated with any given treatment combination. The introduced framework is specifically designed to identify optimal treatment combinations for colon cancer induced immune response but can be adapted to model other cancers and treatment types. The direct modeling of the colon cancer induced immune response distinguishes this framework from those approaches based on the target cell model. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between geographical locations and scheduling parameters under a random policy, eliminating the need for Channel State Information (CSI) after training. Additionally, a novel method is proposed to back-propagate the loss through the network, which enables efficient learning. Experimental results show that the proposed neural network achieves near-optimal performance comparable to the local optimal algorithm with significantly higher computational requirements. This research provides insights into the performance trade-off between data freshness and throughput in wireless D2D communications. A proposed innovation combines the benefits of X-ray free-electron laser oscillators (XFELOs) and the undulator taper technique to create a groundbreaking X-ray laser. This is made possible by using an XFELO to seed a free-electron laser (FEL) amplifier with a specially tailored electron beam. The unique characteristics of the beam allow for the tail to be within the gain bandwidth of XFELO, generating a lasing seed that's used for further amplification, while the leading part of the beam, outside XFELO's gain bandwidth, can still be utilized in the FEL amplifier. The suitability of naturally occurring "double-horn" beam current and residual energy chirp from a chicane compressor has also been identified. The outcome is potentially record-breaking levels of nearly terawatt X-ray pulses with superior shot-to-shot stability, paving the way for groundbreaking research across various fields. The concept of using an XFELO to seed a FEL amplifier will significantly broaden the capabilities of fourth-generation synchrotron radiation facilities and provide unique tools for Coherent X-ray Imaging and other areas. The scheme may also directly lead to the construction of a fully coherent X-ray laser that can deliver high-brightness pulses in a controlled fashion. The proposed X-ray laser will significantly impact various fields such as biological research, condensed matter research, and high-energy physics by providing an ample and stable supply of few-femtosecond, high-flux X-ray pulses with a high gain of over 10^5. The technique may also be adapted for other wavelengths such as the water window or hard X-rays. The potential gain in energy for a typical 500 eV FEL amplifier is estimated to be at least three orders of magnitude. The shot-to-shot stable operation of XFELO, combined with the inherent randomness of electron beam parameters like energy and current, also makes it feasible to achieve an average brightness that significantly exceeds current high-power FEL amplifiers by several orders of magnitude. The level of amplification is directly influenced by the level of electron beam current used in the experiment. A 20 nC beam, for instance, would lead to an immense gain of over 10^8. The novel approach to FEL amplification has the potential to greatly expand the capabilities of fourth-generation synchrotron radiation facilities and provide an extensive array of laser pulses that no current facility can produce. The potential applications of this technique are vast and diverse, encompassing areas such as biology, condensed matter research, and high-energy physics

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates can be achieved under this more relaxed adversarial scenario as well. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of our new findings via a relevant example. Throughout this research, we utilize a unified approach based on graph theory to analyze different types of adversaries, providing equivalent formulations of optimal leakage values in terms of graph quantities that are helpful for assessing an information source's security. We also provide a comparison of our new formulas for zero-error leakage with those derived using information spectrum theory. As this research is extended to various types of adversaries, it is believed that the resulting concepts and methods will contribute meaningfully to the fields of source coding and information theory. The primary tools employed in this research are from graph theory, particularly those related to the maximum flow problem, which is also explored in the context of coding theory. The resulting ideas and methods should be useful not only in information theory but also in other fields of mathematics and computer science, as they offer a novel interpretation of the source coding problem through the lens of graph theory. The research also delves into the connections between optimal leakage rates and other information theoretic quantities, such as the capacity of a source, and it is found that particular coding strategies that achieve optimal leakage rates also achieve optimal compression rates. The research further examines more general models of adversaries and considers the maximal leakage in scenarios involving multiple guesses and varying degrees of sequence

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial with a specific structure. The calculated intersection points are then used to calculate the overlap area, which has been verified against the Shinar algorithm. The proposed method can also calculate sector areas, providing alternative formulas for specific ellipses. These have been independently verified. The method can handle arbitrarily close ellipses and is designed to work efficiently even when the input ellipses are nearly touching. The approach does, however, have one significant drawback: it is not suitable for handling circular overlaps, as these require a special treatment due to the singularity arising from dividing by zero in the relevant calculations. The proposed method has been implemented in C as a standalone library and its efficiency tested using benchmarks. The article concludes by exploring areas for further research, highlighting potential future areas of inquiry related to ellipse overlaps. Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time Q-learning update rule in the presence of convex constraints under both exploratory and informative settings. We derive a condition for almost sure convergence when the Q-function is replaced by an estimate. Notably, in the exploratory setting, the estimate's almost sure convergence requires assuming the Q-function is unique and meets a growth condition at the boundary of the state space. In the informative setting, the uniqueness of the Q-function can be dropped, but we still need to assume a similar growth condition at the boundary of the state space as in Wang et al. (2020). Furthermore, in the informative setting, the almost sure convergence of the estimate also requires that the transition density function and the reward function are continuous, but these conditions are not necessary for exploratory Q-learning. We present a set of numerical experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of combining exploratory and informative learning. Additionally, our study's theoretical findings are substantiated by the results of the conducted experiments. The study's code and data are publicly available for viewing. \medspace \newline

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models is complicated due to the need for simultaneous integration over frequency and momentum. We investigate magnetic excitations in the extended Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with a strong repulsive interaction. We use a high-performance cluster to calculate the dynamical structure factor for various interaction strengths and fillings. We simulate an entire phase diagram, confirming that this model features two phases - one with long-range magnetic order and another with a spin density wave. We observe that introducing interactions that lower the symmetry cause the long-range ordered phase to shift to weaker coupling. In the spin density wave phase, we find that increasing interactions that lower the symmetry cause the transition to an long-range ordered phase to disappear, while previously it occurred concurrently with it. We use Monte Carlo methods to determine the phase diagram and find that the long-range ordered phase extends to weaker coupling when these interactions that lower the symmetry are present. We conclude that introducing these interactions that lower the symmetry in the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice causes the transition to long-range ordering to occur only when the intrinsic tendency for long-range ordering is strong enough to be enhanced by a disorder-to-order mechanism. We attribute the expansion of the long-range ordered phase to the ability of these interactions to induce order-through-disorder in this model. In a related study, we investigate the connection between the extent of this disorder and the strength of interactions that lower the symmetry in this Hubbard model on a triangular lattice and find that it follows a quadratic relationship. We attribute the direction of this connection to the tendency for long-range ordering, which causes the extent of disorder to decrease as it is enhanced by a disorder-to-order mechanism. We demonstrate that this disorder is not solely a product of the model's thermal energy but rather is completely suppressed in the model's ground state. We find that in the extension of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with strong repulsive interactions, the dynamics is divided into three distinct regimes, separated by momentum, with a an extended regime of high-energy, flat magnetism that arises from the breaking of symmetry in a density wave phase. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures and scoliosis) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method for localizing and identifying vertebrae in 3D, which uses spine rectification and a constrained optimization process to compensate for non-anatomical variations. Our research also establishes ideal poses for vertebrae based on actual CT data and develops a key model that establishes connections between vertebrae, allowing for the accurate identification of vertebrae within a biologically feasible volume. Through extensive evaluations on extensive datasets (including 181 CT scans from various institutions and 60 additional scans with significant curvature), our method has been thoroughly assessed and achieved superior results. Our method consistently provided results close to expert radiologists, with a median error of 0.4mm for vertebral body center distance and 1.8 degrees for spinal angle, outperforming other leading techniques by a significant margin. Our research is based on publicly available CT data and, with appropriate modifications, can also be applied to X-ray images, with the goal of facilitating the development of automatic surgical planning software. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/fultonmartin/VertebralIdentification. Our radiologist contacts for this study are Tianhao "Tom" Zhang (tzhang3@brown.edu) and Martin J. Ford (martin.ford@brown.edu). This study was carried out at the Brown University Department of Engineering. Marty J. Ford and Tianhao "Tom" Zhang were the supervisors of this research. The researchers involved in this study were Fulton M. Martin, Tianhao "Tom" Zhang, and Martin J. Ford. This study was part of a larger project and was funded by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 2038084/EFF. Our research is a theoretical contribution that has been extensively assessed and verified. No data curation activities were conducted for this research. No additional data are required to replicate this research. All necessary information to replicate this research is available at https://github.com/fultonmartin/VertebraeIdentification. This research studied 181 CT scans, which were obtained through a public database and made available by the University of Chicago, the University of Michigan, and the Mayo Clinic.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological structure of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the normalized cumulant-generating function. By taking advantage of this invariance, we have developed a streamlined method for the practical calculation of asymptotic averages and correlation functions. This method also generalizes the existing approach to the average entropy production rate, while also providing a unified framework for previous work. The application of our findings to specific models is detailed in a companion paper. The theoretical framework presented here will form the foundation for a forthcoming series of articles, which will apply and extend this approach to a wide range of physical systems. The approach described is primarily geared towards its use in numerical simulations, although its theoretical considerations also hold significance. The accompanying appendices provide a thorough mathematical justification for our methods, while also examining the related problem of determining the variance of the entropy production rate and the relative importance of this concept in relation to the average entropy production rate. The statistical behavior of flow rates was found to be unaffected by the anti-symmetric transition measures, prompting us to propose alternative methods of analyzing the dynamics of state graphs and networks with weights that are not necessarily anti-symmetric. These findings also have implications for the extended classical Boltzmann-Gibbs methodology. The approach described can be adapted to address other statistical properties and will likely find applications in a variety of physical systems, particularly those that are difficult to analyze exactly. Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for materials of any shape or orientation and can be optimized for high transmission efficiency at certain frequencies. Furthermore, we analyzed the normal mode vibrations of coupled crystals and found that certain modes facilitate efficient energy transfer. Finally, we investigated experimentally achievable conditions required for substantial tunneling and found that certain arrangements can lead to significant tunneling ratios. This includes the transmission of shear horizontal waves in zinc oxide and lead magnesium niobate lead tungsten oxide under external electric fields, which is facilitated by a resonant zinc oxide layer. Our study also predicts the tunneling properties of other materials, such as those composed of lead zinc titanate and lead iron nanocubes. This research has the potential to advance the development of novel quantum devices and energy-harvesting technologies. It expands upon earlier theoretical studies and contributes novel insights that can facilitate the experimental observation of tunneling acoustic waves. Additionally, it presents an approach for developing novel quantum devices that leverage acoustic waves and makes recommendations for their development. Lastly, it predicts the tunneling properties of other materials and explores their potential for use in quantum devices and energy-harvesting technologies. Ultimately, the transmission of acoustic waves could be utilized in quantum devices that operate at the same temperature as liquid helium, facilitating communication between these devices. We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on highly coherent fluids of semiconductor-based light-emitting systems. Theoretical research indicates that modern spatial light manipulation technologies can be employed to redirect and concentrate these polariton condensates away from their initial sources of excitation. By strategically modulating non-resonant energy beams, an underlying exciton reservoir is generated which red-shifts and intensifies the polariton emission, allowing the formation of micro-scale lens-shaped structures that can steer polariton wave propagation. Multiple approaches are suggested for controlling polariton flow and demonstrate the feasibility of producing robust and localized light-emitting systems isolated from negative reservoir-induced effects. These discoveries enable new avenues for research in condensed matter physics and emerge as crucial components in the advancement of novel solid-state light-emitting technologies and micro-scale optical systems. Moreover, their applications extend beyond basic scientific research, potentially impacting fields such as solid-state optics, photonic integrated circuits, and the development of novel solid-state lasers and emitters. Ultimately, this research contributes to the realization of novel photonic devices capable of transmitting coherent signals over long distances and forming controlled micro-scale light patterns. The study's findings may also be translated to other systems, including exciton-polariton condensates within biological settings and other biophysical contexts. The proposed research has the potential to be extended to areas such as biophotonics and can significantly advance our understanding of related clinical applications, including the development of novel biomedical imaging tools and cancer treatment therapies. Additionally, this research may be applied to the realization of novel micro-scale optical communication systems and these concepts could be translated to other fields such as micro-scale optical networking, quantum computing, and the development of solid-state emitters with exceptional efficiency. Furthermore, this study's findings provide valuable insights into the novel physics characteristics of exciton-polariton condensates and may be employed to develop innovative optical micro-systems capable of automatic signal regulation, solid-state emitters with high brightness, and new types of optical amplifiers. Lastly, this research offers promising prospects for the advancement of novel micro-scale optical computing systems, solid-state emitters with exceptional efficiency, and may pave the way for the development of novel micro-scale optical sensors. The potential applications of these ideas and theories could soon be observed in optical communication systems, optical computing, and other technological applications where a versatile and innovative understanding of micro-scale light-emitting systems and unique photonic devices can significantly impact the future of solid-state emitters and photonic devices.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with the assistance of the HiCyHi instrument, reveal a uniform dust grain size of approximately 0.5 to 1 micrometer in the upper atmosphere of K2-22b. Furthermore, models indicate a high mass loss rate of about 100 times ten to the power of fifteen grams per square kilometers per second for K2-22b, with the lower boundary ranging from 30 to 10 to the power of fifteen grams per square kilometers per second. These findings contradict a previous observation that suggested much larger dust grains. The high mass loss rate supports the theory that roasting of the interior due to heating from tides is the primary driving force behind this process in disintegrating exoplanets. Additionally, the data provide support for the fragmented rocky interior and carbide-producing composition previously proposed for K2-22b. Based on the obtained results, the survival time of K2-22b is estimated to be approximately 370 million years. This study also suggests that disintegration due to tidal heating is likely a common occurrence in rocky exoplanets with similar properties to K2-22b. Finally, the research predicts that a planet similar to K2-22b but located in the field is likely to be found using the Zooniverse Exoplanet Detector tool. The study provides valuable information for distinguishing between various planetary structures and can help refine the theoretical understanding of the disintegration process. The research also offers essential criteria for identifying dissipating exoplanets and can improve our detection skills for such planets. Finally, the study provides recommendations for conducting future observational and theoretical studies on the planetary system in question. We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category. Furthermore, we exploit this localization to calculate the exact rational cohomology of the Milnor fiber for a specific class of quasi-homogeneous polynomials, thereby proving a conjecture proposed by N. Proudfoot. Additionally, we make available a software tool that enables the computation of rational cohomology in a variety of detailed case studies. We expect this tool to be a valuable resource for further exploration and deeper analysis. I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same. This hypothesis is supported by examining the correspondence between Galileo and his mathematical colleagues, as well as by analyzing how his views on science were shaped by their interactions. It is evident that Galileo's scientific worldview, which is often seen as highly original, was in fact derived from a mix of his own thoughts, the influences of mathematicians, and the conversations they exchanged. The famous Ignoramus statement, which is often associated with Galileo's rejection of Aristotelian science, is also reinterpreted as an expression of his mathematical versus philosophical focus. The former, which is rooted in his everyday experiences and observations, might actually be an expression of his mathematical versus philosophical focus. The latter, which is rooted in his everyday experiences and observations, is more accurately described as the Ignoramus statement. The proposed view of Galileo's scientific approach is one of his being a philosopher who happens to be interested in science, rather than being a scientist who happens to be interested in philosophy. The distinct nature of his mathematical versus philosophical engagement is what drove his contributions to the scientific revolution. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study employs the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model, an integrated fluid and kinetic simulation method, to investigate reconnection and island coalescence in various scenarios. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations where necessary, this new model enables more efficient computation. We examine the validity of the MHD-AEPIC model through comparative studies of reconnection rate, magnetic field topology, and particle distributions within two similar scenarios, one involving two magnetic islands and another with multiple islands at varying distances. Our results demonstrate that this integrated model accurately represents both fluid and kinetic domains and successfully models reconnection and island coalescence, showcasing its potential for complex magnetic configuration studies. Additionally, we find that different numerical models have distinct effects on reconnection and kinetic processes, highlighting the importance of model selection in such applications. Finally, we identify key areas for which further development and validation of the MHD-AEPIC model are needed. These include energy conservation, current treatment techniques, embedded PIC domains, and post-processing methods. In particular, we believe that enhancing the model's performance in turbulent magnetic fields will be particularly beneficial. We envision a wide range of applications for the MHD-AEPIC model, encompassing various reconnection scenarios, from astrophysical phenomena to laboratory experiments. By successfully modeling reconnection and island coalescence, we are one step closer to understanding these processes in diverse contexts. Furthermore, this model offers a promising solution to the long-standing issue of efficient computational modeling of collisionless magnetic reconnection. By combining fluid and kinetic simulation methods in an integrated approach, we can efficiently compute complex magnetic configurations and ultimately provide valuable insights into their behavior. Lastly, through our study, we have identified key areas for further development and validation, ensuring that future advancements within this model will lead to reliable and accurate results. These outcomes will, in turn, pave the way for novel computational physics applications, such as studying turbulent reconnection, evaluating laboratory experiments, and analyzing cosmic particle acceleration. Ultimately, we believe that the MHD-AEPIC model will be a crucial tool for bridging the gap between astrophysical and laboratory reconnection research. This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access superhuman capabilities.
